title: Does Marvin Harrison Jr. Make the Texans a Playoff Team?
summary: Last Saturday morning, rampant speculation surrounding Arizona Cardinals and their embattled wide receiver, Marvin Harrison Jr., reached a peak following ESPN’s Adam Schefter cryptic Saturday morning tweet announcing that Harrison was being traded, but with no mention as to where he was going. Rumors connecting Harrison and the Cardinals to the Houston Texans flooded the […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 04: Marvin Harrison Jr. #18 of the Arizona Cardinals makes a catch for a touchdown against Deonte Banks #2 of the New York Giants during the first quarter at MetLife Stadium on October 04, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last Saturday morning, rampant speculation surrounding Arizona Cardinals and their embattled wide receiver, Marvin Harrison Jr., reached a peak following ESPN’s Adam Schefter cryptic Saturday morning tweet announcing that Harrison was being traded, but with no mention as to where he was going. Rumors connecting Harrison and the Cardinals to the Houston Texans flooded the internet and social media immediately after the announcement. Then, following the Texans’ 26-3 victory over the Tennessee Titans, head coach DeMeco Ryans took some time in the post-game press conference to address the rumors – Marvin Harrison Jr. was, in fact, coming in Houston: When #Texans HC DeMeco Ryans was asked about the trade rumors regarding WR Marvin Harrison Jr rumors: You guys wanna know? We traded for Marvin Harrison. pic.twitter.com/WdFHmeUDZh — DJ Bien-Aime | NASM CPT (@Djbienaime) October 11, 2026 After it was all said and done, the full trade terms included the Cardinals packaging Harrison and a 2027 sixth-round pick in exchange for Houston’s 2027 second and seventh-round picks. I can’t think of a trade announcement quite as peculiar or as…staggered , as this one, but no matter! Marvin Harrison Jr., seen as one of college football’s premier wideouts just a few short years ago and the fourth-overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, is now a Houston Texan! Harrison’s career statistics in Arizona were: 2024: 17 Games (16 Starts), 62 Recs on 116 Tgts (53.4 Ctch%), 885 Yards, 8 TDs, 77.7 PFF Grade (77.2 RECV, 78.8 DROP, 45.4 FUM, 64.0 RBLK) 2025: 12 Games (10 Starts), 41 Recs on 73 Tgts (56.2 Ctch%), 608 Yards, 4 TDs, 68.4 PFF Grade (67.6 RECV, 47.7 DROP, 78.3 FUN, 59.9 RBLK) 2026: 4 Games (4 Starts), 5 Recs on 13 Tgts (38.5 Ctch%), 85 Yards, 1 TD, 52.4 PFF Grade (51.9 RECV, 29.2 DROP, 68.0 FUM, 60.7 RBLK) Marvin Harrison Jr., son of hall-of-fame wide receiver Marvin Harrison, was drafted fourth overall by the Cardinals because they saw him as a player they could sculpt their entire offense around. Coming out of Ohio State, Harrison appeared to be the next in a long line of athletic, dominant NFL receivers that cut their teeth in Columbus. His wingspan and exceptional route-running abilities made Harrison a favorite target of former Ohio State QBs Kyle McCord and current Texans signal-caller CJ Stroud. who is no doubt a bit cheesed by this development: #Texans QB1 C.J. Stroud reacts to the trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. https://t.co/AazUSJ9Xvj pic.twitter.com/XDK9lN1Zbg — Aaron Wilson (@AaronWilson_NFL) October 11, 2026 In short, Marvin Harrison Jr. was nearly impossible to cover in college. But, part of the reason we’re even talking about him joining the Texans is because of his continued struggles in translating that collegiate dominance to the NFL level. Even though Harrison had over 800 receiving yards and eight touchdowns as a rookie, his lack of breakaway speed was something that opposing defenders could adjust to and eventually take advantage of, which is exactly what they did. In several of his games in 2025 and in 2026, Harrison can be seen losing to opposing cornerbacks and failing to use his frame to box out defenders who are more than willing to park themselves directly on top of him. Still, he matched Cardinals WRs Larry Fitzgerald and Anquan Boldin’s rookie touchdown receptions record, so he’s clearly not a complete bust. Following that year, Harrison tallied 608 yards and four touchdowns in an injury-plagued 2025 season, where his yards per receptions went up dramatically, but both his targets and time spent fully healthy dropped in comparable fashion. When healthy, Harrison failed use his big body to enforce his will upon opposing defenders, and in time, the controversy surrounding his drops began to grow. Finally, in 2026, Harrison’s usage in Arizona has fallen off of a cliff. First-year head coach Mike LaFleur, offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett, and QB Jacoby Brissett had all but given up on the Harrison connection before ever delivering on its potential. But, how will he fit into Houston’s offense? Well, this is where a very interesting discussion has kickstarted on Texans Twitter: Nico Collins yards per route run: On ball – 2.2 Off ball – 4.1 They traded for Marv so Nico could play Z full time. — Brett Kollmann (@BrettKollmann) October 12, 2026 "This might be the role for Marvin Harrison Jr., just a high end 2." 👀 @Nate_Tice and @HaydenWinks break down MHJ's role on the Texans offense. (via Football 301) pic.twitter.com/i6mTH7Y8p6 — Yahoo Sports (@YahooSports) October 12, 2026 There’s disagreement afoot about what position Harrison will primarily play with the Texans: As the big, outside-the-Numbers “X” receiver, or the more motion heavy, off-ball “Z” receiver. Harrison has the prototypical X receiver size, strength, and route acumen, but he lacks the speed and hands that Nico Collins possesses. That being said, Collins’ speed and acceleration make him a more ideal receiver for the Z spot, but making Harrison the X receiver in his first action as a Texan – who are in very dire straits themselves – may be a little too much to ask, even of a former fourth-overall pick. If I were to throw my two cents in, I’d say that we’re going to get a little bit of both from each receiver, meaning that Harrison and Collins will trade spots on the field, sub in and out for each other, and will be treated as a sort of 1A and 1B for this passing offense as a whole. Texans offensive coordinator Nick Caley, a fruit of the Josh McDaniels/Patriots offensive tree, has already shown interest in moving receivers around and placing them into different positions on the field. I believe that he and Stroud are salivating at the concept of using both receivers on the field at the same time, and will experiment with pre-snap motion with both receivers to further confuse opposing defenses. Having Harrison Jr. on the team also grants Caley the opportunity to use two bona fide outside receivers on the field at the same time. You could argue the Texans already had something like that with Collins and Xavier Hutchinson, but Hutchinson does not possess the footwork and outside-the-numbers acumen that Harrison has. Harrison is a threat at all three levels of the passing game, and he and Stroud had an exceptional connection on mid-range in-breaking routes while in college. On top of that, one of Harrison’s strengths is chasing the deep-ball, which just so happens to be one of CJ Stroud’s best traits in his NFL career. If Stroud, Caley, and the Texans offensive staff can work together to get Harrison and Collins banging on all cylinders at the same time, they’ll be a very, very hard offense to stop. Although, all of these hypotheticals are predicated on the idea of the trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. working out in favor of the Texans, and there is no guarantee that this trade will work. Ask any Cardinals fan, and they’ll tell you of a big-time drop by Harrison, or a game where he needed to show up and just…didn’t. Revenge of the Bird’s Barry Shuck summed it up well in his analysis of the trade: “Harrison just couldn’t get himself open. That is the bottom line. Yes, he had 10 drops in the 30 games he started, but while playing for Arizona, Harrison ranked dead last in the league among all receivers (with 50 targets or more over the past three years) in separation, averaging just 2.1 yards of separation when targeted, per NFL Next Gen Stats . That is a huge stat, and very telling. Brissett just couldn’t count on Harrison getting open, so he threw the ball to the ones who were getting more than a step on their defender. And does anyone consider Harrison explosive enough? Explosive at all?…

title: Five Good Texans Questions with Big Cat Country
summary: Stay in this business long enough and you get to know the people on the other side. That is particularly true within the AFC South when we have these games twice a season. Gus Logue of Big Cat Country and I have been doing this for all five seasons that I have been doing five […]
full_text: LONDON, ENGLAND - OCTOBER 11: Parker Washington of the Jacksonville Jaguars celebrates scoring his teams first touchdown during the 2026 NFL London Games match between Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on October 11, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Ryan Pierse/Getty Images) | Getty Images Stay in this business long enough and you get to know the people on the other side. That is particularly true within the AFC South when we have these games twice a season. Gus Logue of Big Cat Country and I have been doing this for all five seasons that I have been doing five questions. The Jaguars have become the chief rival for the Texans as it pertains to the playoffs and this year is no different. This time the interdivision battle goes to London. The 4-1 Jaguars stand between the Texans and getting back into the playoff conversation. We started with the London angle. Battle Red Blog: Jacksonville has been the unofficial home team in London for several years. Do you see that giving them key advantages on Sunday? Gus Logue: Not really. Jacksonville was the “home” team in last week’s game against Philadelphia, but it seemed like Eagles fans outnumbered Jaguars fans 10-to-1. The familiarity of traveling overseas could be an edge, but really, the Jaguars’ biggest advantage this week is the simple fact that they’re already in London. The Texans still have to cross an ocean and acclimate themselves to a new continent. After the win against the Eagles, Liam Coen said, “We really didn’t get to practice hard last week. It was one of those weird weeks, because we were a little nicked up, and then you got the travel.” I expect the Jaguars to play a cleaner game against the Texans than they did against the Eagles, even with Houston being the tougher opponent. BRB: It’s year two of the Travis Hunter experience. How is that going? How is the breakdown between offensive and defensive snaps looking? GL: It is going GREAT, thank you for asking! After playing 67% of offensive snaps and 36% of defensive snaps as a rookie, Hunter is now being deployed full-time as a starting cornerback while seeing a couple of offensive snaps per game. He had a 1st down catch on an option route last week. His defensive tape is highly encouraging. In the first two weeks of the season, Hunter looked really solid, but a bit hesitant coming back from the knee injury that cut his rookie season short. It didn’t take long for him to get his swagger back, because Hunter has looked like a field-tilting, quarterback-baiting, difference-making CB over the past month. BRB: Are there any new faces in Jacksonville that will have a dramatic impact on the outcome on Sunday? GL: All-Pro long snapper Ross Matiscik was injured last week, so the Jaguars will be flying someone in to fill his spot (though nose tackle DaVon Hamilton filled in very admirably). I don’t know who Matiscik’s replacement is quite yet, but beyond that spot, keep an eye on rookie receiver Josh Cameron. He hasn’t quite out-snapped Brian Thomas Jr., but it wouldn’t be bold to say he is outplaying him. It’s also worth shouting out running back Bhayshul Tuten and Ventrell Miller, as they have been everything Jacksonville could’ve hoped for after letting Travis Etienne and Devin Lloyd walk in free agency. PFF has Tuten and Miller graded as the top players at their respective positions this season. BRB: How do you see the AFC South race shaping up? Secondarily, which divisional opponent do Jags fans enjoy beating the most? GL: I agree with the popular take that Houston is better than their record and remains a threat to win the division. But it’s hard not to feel confident about the Jaguars, given they’ve already built a three-game lead over the Texans during the toughest part of their season. (The Colts and Titans are dog water.) I expect Jacksonville to repeat as AFC South champs, and Houston to sneak into the playoffs as a Wild Card team. It helps that the AFC West isn’t as deep as expected. Even if the Jaguars sweep the Texans in the regular season, I will be praying to the football gods that Will Anderson Jr. does not make it far in the bracket. We despise the Titans. They were the only team to defeat the Jaguars during their incredible 1999 season — and they did it three times! Plus, Derrick Henry (a Jacksonville native) embarrassed us plenty of times. We hate that Peyton Manning and Andrew Luck ran the division for so long, and the current rivalry with Houston is legit a great one, but we will always enjoy beating the Titans more than any other team. BRB: The Jags opened as 2.5 point favorites according to Fanduel. Do you see the Jags covering that? Are there any prop bets you feel comfortable recommending? GL: I think that if this game were played out 10 times, the Jaguars would win and cover the spread in 6 or 7 of those scenarios. So I’ll pick them to cover but without much confidence. A healthy Nico Collins and a rejuvenated Marvin Harrison Jr. could cause serious issues for Jacksonville’s secondary, and we all know the threat that Houston’s defense poses against suspect offensive lines. Woody Marks under 47.5 rushing yards is an easy recommendation, considering Jacksonville has allowed 45 rushing yards total over the past two weeks. They join the 1969 Dallas Cowboys as the only Super Bowl-era teams to not allow an opposing player to rush for 40+ yards in their first five games of a season. We really think Marks is gonna be the first? I do expect big performances from C.J. Stroud and Jaguars tight end Brenton Strange (over 37.5 receiving yards looks nice). Score prediction: Jaguars 20, Texans 16. We want to thank Gus so much for his time an attention to this feature. These interchanges are always interesting because the people involved are always so nice and accommodating even when the games themselves are tense. We want to wish Gus and the Jaguars the best of luck for the rest of the season. As per usual, we hope that the luck begins on Monday morning.

title: How much is Jonathan Taylor worth on the trade market?
summary: This is the first part of a three-article series looking at the hypothetical trade value of three of the Colts’ biggest stars. We’re starting with Jonathan Taylor. This is not an argument that Indianapolis should trade any of them. In fact, the answer in most cases will probably be the opposite. The idea is to […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - OCTOBER 11: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts rushes against the Pittsburgh Steelers in the first half at Acrisure Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images This is the first part of a three-article series looking at the hypothetical trade value of three of the Colts’ biggest stars. We’re starting with Jonathan Taylor. This is not an argument that Indianapolis should trade any of them. In fact, the answer in most cases will probably be the opposite. The idea is to look at what would happen if the Colts received serious interest around the trade deadline and determine what each player should realistically be worth. Taylor is the obvious place to start. He is 27 years old, coming off a 1,585-yard season and remains one of the best running backs in football. He has nearly 8,000 career rushing yards, three Pro Bowls and a First-Team All-Pro selection. Even during a relatively inefficient start to 2026, Taylor has six rushing touchdowns through five games and remains the centerpiece of the Colts’ offense. Running backs, however, are difficult to value in trades. The position has been devalued across the league, Taylor has accumulated an enormous workload and a team acquiring him would eventually have to pay the expensive portion of his new contract. So what is he actually worth? The recent trade market gives us a floor and a ceiling There are very few useful running back trades because very few players of Taylor’s caliber ever become available. D’Andre Swift was traded from Detroit to Philadelphia in 2023 for a future fourth-round pick and a swap of seventh-round selections. Swift was only 24 and had averaged 4.6 yards per carry over his first three seasons, but Detroit had just drafted Jahmyr Gibbs and clearly no longer viewed Swift as part of its future. Jay Ajayi provides another useful floor. Philadelphia acquired him from Miami for a fourth-round pick in 2017. Ajayi was also only 24 and was less than a year removed from a 1,272-yard Pro Bowl season. Neither player was Jonathan Taylor. Swift was a good player who had never topped 617 rushing yards in a season before being traded. Ajayi had one excellent season and a much shorter résumé. Taylor has been one of the best running backs in football for most of his career and has already produced multiple seasons that neither player approached. If Swift and Ajayi were worth fourth-round picks, I have a difficult time seeing any scenario where a fourth is enough for Taylor. To me, that establishes the absolute bottom of the conversation rather than his actual value. The much more useful comparison is Christian McCaffrey. San Francisco acquired McCaffrey midway through the 2022 season for a 2023 second-round pick, third-round pick and fourth-round pick, plus a fifth-round pick in 2024. That is obviously a massive haul for a running back, and Taylor probably would not get quite that much. McCaffrey was 26 when San Francisco acquired him, roughly a year younger than Taylor is now, and his receiving ability made him uniquely valuable. He was essentially an elite running back and high-end receiving weapon in one player. Taylor is also carrying considerably more mileage, which becomes important when projecting what a contender would actually be buying. Still, Taylor belongs much closer to the McCaffrey end of this spectrum than the Swift end. How much high-level football does Taylor have left? I have written about the “running back wall” several times because running backs tend to have a much more dramatic decline curve than most positions. In my most recent update , I used approximately 3,300 combined college and NFL touches as the baseline point where heavily used backs tend to begin declining. It is not a magical number where a running back suddenly becomes bad. There is roughly a 600-touch standard deviation around it, meaning some players fall off much earlier and others remain productive well beyond it. Taylor is now around 2,800 combined touches between Wisconsin and Indianapolis. At his current workload, he is on pace for close to 390 touches this season, which would put him a little above 3,100 by the end of the year. Using the 3,300-touch baseline, he would probably reach the historical wall sometime during the 2027 season. That sounds concerning until you put it in the context of a deadline trade. A team acquiring Taylor around the middle of this season would get the remainder of 2026 and all of 2027 before age and workload become a major concern. Even if he crosses the 3,300 threshold sometime next season, that number is an average rather than an expiration date. Taylor is also a better athlete than the average running back included in these studies. I would feel comfortable projecting roughly another season and a half of high-level Taylor, with 2028 becoming the uncertain year. That still has considerable value to a contender. Teams making deadline trades are generally not worried about what a player will look like four years from now. They are trying to win a Super Bowl in the current window. If Denver, Green Bay or another contender believes Taylor could materially improve its chances over the next two postseasons, what happens when he is 30 is not particularly relevant. And even if the decline begins during the back half of the contract, the acquiring team controls him through 2028. Taylor does not have to remain the best running back in football for the entire deal to provide value. His contract is actually helpful for a deadline trade Taylor signed a two-year, $44 million extension before the season that keeps him under contract through 2028. The expensive portion of the new deal essentially begins next year. A team trading for him during 2026 would have a relatively inexpensive immediate cost. Taylor’s 2026 base salary is $6.98 million, and Indianapolis has already paid the signing bonus. An acquiring team would only be responsible for the remaining portion of his base salary and applicable bonuses for the rest of this season rather than taking on the Colts’ prorated signing-bonus charges. That makes fitting him under the cap at the deadline fairly easy. The bigger commitment comes afterward. Taylor is scheduled for roughly $16 million in cash in 2027 and approximately $18 million in 2028. That is premium running back money, but a contender trading meaningful draft capital for Taylor would obviously be doing so because it considers him a premium running back. The contract also provides certainty. A team is not trading a second-round pick for a rental that could leave four months later. It gets Taylor for three playoff pushes. Who could actually want him? There has to be a market for any trade-value projection to make sense, and I can see several teams where Taylor would provide a major upgrade. Denver might be the cleanest fit. The Broncos are 4-2 and have one of the better defenses in football, but the offense remains inconsistent. They managed only 168 total yards in Thursday night’s win over Seattle, with the defense again doing most of the heavy lifting. J.K. Dobbins is their veteran lead back, but his extensive injury history makes him difficult to rely on as the centerpiece of a championship run. Taylor would give Sean Payton a legitimate workhorse and take pressure off Bo Nix on a team that appears capable of winning now. Denver also retains its own first-, second- and third-round picks in 2027, so the draft capital is there. Green Bay is fascinating for a different reason. The Packers have always placed a major emphasis on the running game in recent years, but Josh Jacobs has created uncertainty. He rushed for 929 yards at 4.0 yards per carry last season, a noticeable step down from his best years, and he has yet to play in 2026 after spending the start of the season on the commissioner’s exempt list. He is now eligible to return, but his long-term future in Green Bay is hardly…

title: Which Colts player’s emergence would benefit the team the most?
summary: Without a 1st round pick and the extreme unlikelihood that CIG would allow the movement of their 2nd round pick, there is no reason to expect that a player upgrade might come in from outside of the building and provide a spark. Given that, any improvement in personnel, will have to come from among the […]
full_text: Without a 1st round pick and the extreme unlikelihood that CIG would allow the movement of their 2nd round pick, there is no reason to expect that a player upgrade might come in from outside of the building and provide a spark. Given that, any improvement in personnel, will have to come from among the players in the building. Since I used the word “emergence”, I think we are talking about players who have yet to show themselves as instrumental cogs to this point. I do not want to add “return to form” players, as that would be a separate group of players. On offense, I have two options. Deion Burks could be that field stretcher that the offense is missing during AP’s absence. Treadwell and Allen are nearly the same player and Dulin looks like he may be out again this week. Burks’ speed is well documented, so he has the ability to get behind the secondary, or at least his man. Even if you are only throwing to him 4 or 5 times a game, let him do what Pierce did in the early part of his career, which is run fast and take at least on person with you. He has already shown the ability to run the jet sweep, so if he were to catch a couple of long ones, he could stretch the field both horizontally and vertically. The second is Jalen Travis. His contribution would be in the form of no longer being the weak link on the O-line. He came in last year and you can look at his performance two different ways. His entry into the starting lineup coincided with Daniel Jones going down for the season. He played “admirably”, but his play this year is much closer to Matt Pryor than his counterpart Raimann. He was a 4th round pick, so you may not expect stardom, but we are getting great play from 3rd rounders Raimann and Goncalves along with fellow 4th rounder Bortolini. This may be the one position group that has developed after the draft, so there is hope. His emergence as a trusted rush stopper, would allow Jones more comfort in the pocket and maybe even see him step into more throws. On defense, there are a few players to consider. Starting in the backfield, Haulcey is only five games into his career, so expecting him to be plug and play was optimistic. With Bynum being very good in space, just seeing Haulcey limit the running game and making the QB look away from TEs would be a nice first step to seeing the defense put up more of a fight. He needs time to have the game slow down, but our secondary will not be the weapon that we hoped, until he has caught up. At LB, you could say just about anyone, but it has to be your first pick in the draft, and the hoped leader of the unit on day one. He played less early on, because he was still slowed by an injury and we kept him active to let him see the field on a limited basis. If he could be as good as his draft status suggests, it would be a great elevating ingredient for the entire D. Boettcher could do same, but most would say Allen has the higher ceiling. Seeing both take the job and run with it, would theoretically improve both the run and pass defense exponentially. Helping to limit missed tackles and helping to control the middle of the field in the passing game would both fix existing weaknesses. Lastly, something needs happen with the pass rush. You might point to Latu, but he has at least semi-emerged. That means that it needs to come from the other side, and rather than put that kind of pressure on the late round rookies, I’d tab JTT as the player that needs to fulfill his promise. Not that Latu doesn’t need to step up, but having someone on the other side actually become a problem, is what is needed for Latu to take his next step. JTT is a 2nd round pick, same with Allen. Halcey is a 3rd and Boettcher a 4th, so there has been an investment made in each player. Seeing all of them realize their potential, eliminates a lot of problems on the defensive side of the ball. I believe the defense has the biggest need for improvement, but I doubt that seeing only one of the defensive names that I mentioned actually taking a big step, will be enough to improve the D by enough to make a difference. So, my choice is Burks being the one that most improves the team, should he make a leap. If he can provide some big plays and stretch the field, maybe we can see the offense click enough to need less from the defense. Who is your choice? Quick segment check. I watch more TV, than I follow social media. Yep, I’m old. So, while watching the NFL Network, I saw “Start’em” and “Sit’em” on the crawler at the bottom of the screen. I do not know the name of the person that actually puts their name on these, so it could have easily been someone that got stuck with the role, maybe even the tech that creates the crawler? This is intended as advice for Fantasy players. Anyway, this is what it said: Start’em: Carnell Tate, Tyler Warren, and Spencer Shrader. Seeing Warren on the list is good, but Shrader being on the list, suggest we will struggle getting into the end zone and Tate being on there might indicate that we are in for another long day against a receiver that we have no answer for. Sit’em: Treadwell, Cam Ward and the Colts D. Yikes! Not a good look when you are facing the offense that is dead last in yards gained and points scored, and you are being advised that the Colts D may not be able to stop them! The whole thing looks conflicted. You do not think that their QB will play well, but that one of his receivers will? How should our D be that bad, if we force their QB into a bad fantasy day?

Slayton was signed on September 22nd following Alec Pierce’s week two injury that sent him to injured reserve. There was some hope that Slayton could come in and become a downfield option that the Colts lacked with […]
full_text: New York Giants wide receiver Darius Slayton had a rough Week 9. Syndication The Record | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co In what now seems like a very odd series of event the Indianapolis Colts have released Darius Slayton. We have released WR Darius Slayton. — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 16, 2026 Slayton was signed on September 22nd following Alec Pierce’s week two injury that sent him to injured reserve. There was some hope that Slayton could come in and become a downfield option that the Colts lacked with Pierce out. In the end the Colts move on from Slayton without him ever appearing in a single game for the horseshoe. Slayton was never going to be a revelation for a receiver corps struggling to produce week in and week out but at this point any veteran help they could get was being welcomed. Afterall, get a guy into a game and you never know, it’s possible he could have a game or make even a single play that could get Indy a win they otherwise wouldn’t have gotten. Instead the Colts move on and this brief signing will be nothing more than an answer to a weird Colts trivia question a decade from now. The question now becomes, how do they fill this roster spot? It seems that tight end Will Mallory is close to making his return and while most probably would not love the move Anthony Gould keeps bouncing between the practice squad and being elevated for gameday, so that move could make some sense. What is unlikely is that there is any sort of needle moving transaction coming for the Indianapolis Colts, at least not until the offseason. Check back in to see who fills out the 53.
author: Chris Shepherd

title: Jaguars vs. Texans: Staff roundtable and game picks for Week 6
summary: Welcome to Big Cat Country’s staff roundtable! This week, we’re previewing the Jacksonville Jaguars’ first divisional matchup and second London game of the season. They’ll face the Houston Texans in what will surely be a scrappy, hard-fought bout. Question 1: What’s your top question/concern about the Jaguars this week? Dillon Appleman: The offensive line is […]
full_text: Sep 21, 2025; Jacksonville, Florida, USA; Houston Texans wide receiver Nico Collins (12) is tackled by Jacksonville Jaguars defensive back Travis Hunter (12) at EverBank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Morgan Tencza-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to Big Cat Country’s staff roundtable! This week, we’re previewing the Jacksonville Jaguars’ first divisional matchup and second London game of the season. They’ll face the Houston Texans in what will surely be a scrappy, hard-fought bout. Question 1: What’s your top question/concern about the Jaguars this week? Dillon Appleman : The offensive line is easily my biggest concern for obvious reasons. The line already hadn’t been playing at a very high level through the first five weeks, and now the unit just lost its most reliable piece: left tackle Anton Harrison. The Jags are lucky to have an experienced backup like Walker Little to fill that spot, but he’ll need some help on Sunday if the team is going to keep the Texans’ pass rush at bay. Travis Holmes : It’s impossible to overstate my concerns about the task ahead for this Jacksonville offensive line. The Jaguars are facing one of the league’s top teams in sacks without their starting right tackle and with a left guard who is limited at best after spending the week on the injury report, plus a center, right guard, and right tackle who have all struggled to some degree in 2026. This feels like a recipe for a gift-wrapped seven-sack performance, much like the one the Seahawks defense delivered in 2025. With potential leaks at any of the five positions and tight end Nate Boerkircher also nursing a back issue, bullets could be flying at Trevor Lawrence from every angle on Sunday. Gus Logue : My biggest concern this week is easily the Harrison-less offensive line, so I’ll frame my biggest question differently: How aggressive will DeMeco Ryans be after taking over defensive playcalling duties for the Texans defense last week? Like many disciples of the Cover 3-heavy system originally popularized by the Legion of Boom, Ryans prefers a “Pros vs. Joes” philosophy rather than being an “Xs and Os” connoisseur. He deploys relatively basic defensive structures to allow his ultra-talented players to play fast and physical. Even without Harrison available, the Jaguars will have a good chance to win if Ryans calls defensive plays the way he always has — but if he decides to turn up the pressure dial and throw in some creative blitzes rather than allowing Jacksonville to double-team Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter all game, Trevor Lawrence could be in trouble. I don’t think the Jags have to “beat” Anderson Jr. and Hunter, but they do have to beat the blitz. Henry Zimmer : I am going to be so bold as to say the offensive line is going to be a huge concern this week. Will Anderson Jr. is playing out of his mind, and now it is up to the likes of Cole Van Lanen and Walker Little to stop him. Oh brother. Question 2: What’s the key to a Jaguars victory this week? Dillon : 1st down success on both sides of the ball. On offense, getting chunk gains on 1st down would go a long way in ensuring those Texans pass rushers can’t just tee off in obvious passing downs. On defense, the run defense isn’t in question, but I wouldn’t count on the Texans to test that unit much on Sunday. That means the quick pass game on 1st down will be key for them. Gotta prevent easy slants and screens on early downs. Travis : Whether Jacksonville can stop the run when Houston leans on its jumbo personnel packages featuring six or more offensive linemen. In Week 5, the Texans used their jumbo look on 1/4 plays against Tennessee, running the ball on 81% of those snaps with a success rate just over 44%. This closely mirrors what the Texans did during Davis Mills’ 19-point comeback against the Jaguars last season. Houston’s running backs finished that day with 19 carries for 110 yards and a touchdown. A 5.8-yard-per-carry average is winning football, and I expect Houston to try the same approach on Sunday to keep Jacksonville’s defense honest. Whichever offense can establish the run against these dominant defensive fronts will clearly have the edge in this matchup. Gus : Winning the redzone battle. Both of these offenses should find success in the middle of the field and put together lengthy drives, so the result will come down to execution in scoring territory. Who makes more hero throws on the run between Trevor Lawrence and C.J. Stroud? Who puts the ball in harm’s way more often? Which receivers come down with the 50/50 jump balls? Which cornerbacks break it up? Which defensive line makes the goal-line stand? Jacksonville will certainly look to improve from its redzone showing against Philadelphia last week. Henry : If the Jags can get the ball safely and effectively out of Trevor Lawrence’s hands before that pass rush gets home, this is a very winnable game. The secondary for the Texans isn’t excellent (23rd in pass defense), so you can easily have winnable matchups there. If the time is provided, of course. Question 3: Who will be an X-factor for the Jaguars this week ? Dillon : I’m sure the offensive line will be a popular answer here, but I’m going to go with Travis Hunter. The Texans have no run game, so I’m expecting a heavy dose of Nico Collins on Sunday. It’ll be an interesting stylistic matchup for Hunter when he’s lined up with the imposing Collins, but I think he’ll have opportunities to make a play on the ball and potentially create a turnover. Travis : Whether for better or worse, Sunday’s X-factor for Jacksonville will be starting left tackle Walker Little. If he can somehow pull a 2022 playoff-caliber performance out of his bag and replicate what he did against Khalil Mack, it would go a long way toward helping the Jaguars walk away with a victory. However, if Little struggles and needs consistent help to slow down Will Anderson Jr. (7.5 sacks) and/or Danielle Hunter (3 sacks), Jacksonville’s passing game may never get out of the park. Gus : Jacksonville’s new starting running back has been as good as we could’ve hoped to start this season. According to NFL Pro, Bhayshul Tuten has forced a missed tackle on 37.0% of his carries (the fourth-highest rate among 40 qualifying RBs) and 47.2% of his rushing yards have come after forcing a missed tackle (the second-highest rate). But Houston’s defense ranks second this season with 3.3 yards allowed per designed run and 3.6 yards per missed tackle on running back runs. Can Tuten continue putting the rushing offense on his back? Or will the Texans’ defense prove to be too much? Henry : Despite me talking about tackles earlier, I am going to say Robert Hainsey is the X-Factor this week. There was something very wrong between Hainsey, Lawrence, and Liam Coen last week. That needs to be super clean and crisp so the Jags don’t rack up another week full of procedural penalties. If the Jags are going to go to a quick game to avoid Anderson and Danielle Hunter, it starts with Hainsey. Final score prediction? Legendary tight end Travis Kelce re-signed with the team this offseason with that in mind. Once that mission is complete, Kelce’s off-field talents could be in very high demand in 2027. The latest Kansas City Chiefs news There could be a three-way bidding war for Kansas City Chiefs TE Travis Kelce, and it has nothing to do with him on the football field | A to Z Sports “Last year, Travis Kelce and Greg Olsen were inquiring with Amazon about whether or not the Prime Video spot would be available this year, and Kirk Herbstreit was still under contract,” Mike Florio said on Pardon My Take. “So, Kelce was looking at this last year. He’s already got the relationship with Amazon with New Heights, but his brother’s already got the relationship in place with ESPN, and he’s going to be the one. “He’s going to be the one they all want. And as it stands, CBS is going to be looking, ESPN is going to be looking, and Prime Video did that extension with Herbstreit, which basically has a clause that says if we find anyone better, we can tear up your contract. So there could be a three-way bidding war for Travis Kelce, and I think they’re all going to want him. And I think he’s going to be in a booth somewhere next year.” Chiefs punter Matt Araiza off to great start by using legs in more ways than one | The Kansas City Star “I couldn’t believe it, because … I sprinted downfield to cover (on the punt that was blown dead by penalty),” Araiza said. “So I’m dead tired. My cardio is not very good. I don’t really work on it that much. I get back to the line of scrimmage, thinking, ‘What do I want to do? Hit the ball in the same direction, maybe switch it up? “And then I see the look, and I’m like, ‘No way.’ Sure enough, it worked out.” One big key to the fake’s success was how Araiza sold a punt look to the Raiders upon taking the snap from James Winchester. Two Bold Predictions for the Kansas City Chiefs vs. Los Angeles Chargers in Week 6 | Athlon Sports Bold Prediction No. 1: Running Back Emmett Johnson Sees Largest Workload The Chiefs have been singing the fifth-round pick’s praise since training camp. He has done everything the team has asked and done it well. However, with running back Kenneth Walker III running all over opposing defenses, Johnson has just 16 rushes for 56 yards and five receptions for 74 yards. The Chiefs have hinted that a larger role was coming for the rookie, but it hasn’t happened yet. Chiefs nose tackle Khyiris Tonga is playing almost as much offense as Travis Hunter | Pro Football Talk Jaguars cornerback/wide receiver Travis Hunter has been much-hyped for his status as a two-way player, first as a Heisman Trophy winner at Colorado and now in the NFL. But there’s another two-way player in the NFL this season who hasn’t received as much hype: Chiefs nose tackle and fullback Khyiris Tonga. Like Hunter, Tonga has started every game on defense this season. Like Hunter, Tonga has played only limited offensive snaps this season. Tonga has two carries; Hunter has two catches. Both have picked up one first down. Hunter plays a little bit more on offense, but not much more: Hunter has played 6.8 percent of the Jaguars’ offensive snaps, while Tonga has played 4.2 percent of the Chiefs’ offensive snaps. Around the NFL Broncos’ Jonathon Cooper removed from NFL commissioner’s exempt list, can play in Week 7 | The Athletic The NFL has removed Denver Broncos outside linebacker Jonathon Cooper from the commissioner’s exempt list, making him eligible to play when the team travels to face the Arizona Cardinals in Week 7. Cooper, 28, was placed on the list Aug. 30 and was ineligible to play or practice with the team during the first six weeks of the season. His placement on the list was the result of two June arrests stemming from a pair of domestic incidents with his then-girlfriend. Cooper is facing multiple charges, including a second-degree felony assault charge, and is currently scheduled for a trial date in March. Packers’ Josh Jacobs eligible to return next week amid investigation | ESPN The league’s investigation into Jacobs under the personal conduct policy remains ongoing, however, leaving open the possibility that he could still be suspended. When he comes off the list next week, Jacobs will have missed the first six games of the season, and those games would count toward any suspension. However, if Jacobs ends up getting suspended for more than six games, he will have to miss additional games to make up the difference. Sources: Eagles’ Jalen Hurts, out indefinitely with blood clot, not planned for IR | ESPN Hurts and the Eagles are still gathering more information and seeking additional medical opinions, with the quarterback’s health the foremost consideration. They believe the blood clot is treatable, with Hurts trying to determine the best course, sources said. The ultimate decision about when Hurts returns to play will come from his medical team, and the Eagles are ready to follow his lead. There is still a chance Hurts eventually ends up on injured reserve, if that is the direction the medical information leads them. In most cases, blood clots are treated with anticoagulants, otherwise known as blood thinners. A player cannot play while on blood thinners. We harp on that here. We guilt those guys into being physical because when they’re not, we put it on tape. And I just think that’s him, he plays that way. Whatever the shoulder and everything, I think he’s kind of put it out of his mind, which is a good thing. title: Chiefs-Chargers Week 6 final injury report: Rashee Rice out
summary: Each practice day this season, the Kansas City Chiefs release an official injury report ahead of the next game. In Week 6, the Chiefs host the Los Angeles Chargers for a divisional matchup on Sunday afternoon. Here is the Chiefs’ final official injury report of the week, courtesy of the team’s official website. The chart is […]
full_text: (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Each practice day this season, the Kansas City Chiefs release an official injury report ahead of the next game. In Week 6, the Chiefs host the Los Angeles Chargers for a divisional matchup on Sunday afternoon. Here is the Chiefs’ final official injury report of the week, courtesy of the team’s official website . The chart is courtesy of Chiefs Senior Reporter Matt McMullen on X . Chiefs Wide receiver Rashee Rice (Hamstring) was ruled out after missing every practice this week. Here is the information head coach Andy Reid provided on Friday. “He’s out there and wanting to jump in on everything; he’ll be alright,” Reid said. “You never know about these things, but he’s a pretty fast healer.” Left tackle Josh Simmons (Back) was ruled out after limited participation in practice all week. Reid shared an update on Simmons’ progress during his press conference on Friday. “He has been getting better as we go here,” Reid said. “He got some work in; he didn’t work in the team periods, but that was the idea… to get some base under him, some fundamentals and technique and start getting that back.” “He was excited to be out there, just to be back with the guys on the field instead of the meeting room,” Reid continued. Cornerback L’Jarius Sneed (Knee) was listed as questionable after limited participation in practice for three consecutive days. His time on the field is regularly managed due to a lingering knee issue, but he doesn’t always carry a tag into the game like he will this week. Defensive tackle Peter Woods (Neck) did not carry a game designation after a full practice on Friday; he was suddenly a limited participant on Thursday. Chargers The Chargers’ injuries are headlined by starting right tackle Joe Alt (Neck), who will miss his second consecutive game after suffering the injury in Week 4 against the Seattle Seahawks . Left guard Kayode Awosika (Fibula) will also remain sidelined; he played 85 snaps at the position over Weeks 1 and 2. Los Angeles’ offense will also be missing wide receiver Tre Harris, who has led the Chargers’ offense in wideout snaps so far this season (232). He leads the team in receptions (15) and receiving yards (225). Chargers HC Jim Harbaugh on if he anticipates a snap count on WR Ladd McConkey (foot) or WR Quentin Johnston (chest): "I don't know." on if they're full-go: "We'll see how it goes." pic.twitter.com/ahYV5ZgnwE — Alex Insdorf (@alexinsdorf99) October 16, 2026 Head coach Jim Harbaugh said, “We’ll see how it goes,” when asked if starting wide receivers Ladd McConkey (Foot) and Quentin Johnston (Chest) were full-go, per Alex Insdorf on X . Fullback Alec Ingold (Shoulder) was placed on the Reserve/Injured list this week. On defense, Los Angeles will be without safety Derwin James Jr. (Hamstring) and cornerback Donte Jackson (Hamstring). James hasn’t played since Week 3, but he has 21 tackles and a pass defended this year. Jackson has played the third-most snaps at outside cornerback for the Chargers this season, behind Cam Hart and Tarheeb Still. Cornerback Rodney Shelley (Hamstring) and wide receiver Brenen Thompson (quadriceps) are doubtful . Shelley is a reserve outside cornerback, while the rookie wideout from Mississippi State has just one 13-yard catch this year. The Chargers’ defensive line will feature three players questionable to play: Jamaree Caldwell (Knee), Bud Dupree (Neck) and Dalvin Tomlinson (Hamstring). Caldwell leads the unit in interior snaps this year, but Tomlinson has also been an important interior piece when he’s on the field. Dupree has two pressures (one quarterback hit) over 32 pass-rush snaps on the edge this season. Linebacker Daiyan Henley (Knee) is also questionable ; he has the second-most snaps (291) on the Chargers’ defense this season and leads the team in tackles. Wide receiver KeAndre Lambert-Smith (Hamstring) is questionable to play; he would need to be activated off the Reserve/Injured list before Sunday, as he has not appeared in a game this season.

title: Chiefs-Chargers: 5 questions with Bolts From The Blue ahead of Week 6
summary: On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs face the Los Angeles Chargers in the late window of Week 6 games. We welcome Michael Peterson of Bolts From the Blue — our sister SBNation site covering the Chargers— for Five Questions with the Enemy. Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device and join the Bolts […]
full_text: Credit: Jay Biggerstaff-Imagn Images On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs face the Los Angeles Chargers in the late window of Week 6 games. We welcome Michael Peterson of Bolts From the Blue — our sister SBNation site covering the Chargers— for Five Questions with the Enemy . Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app! Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time. Chat live throughout the game Browse with fewer ads Easily jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device and join the Bolts From the Blue community through Sunday’s game to get perspectives from both sides of the Week 4 matchup! 1. The Chargers entered this season following consecutive 11-6 finishes, but they are now 0-5 and one of only three winless teams remaining. How has this start changed the expectations surrounding Jim Harbaugh and the team for the rest of the season? The new expectation now is that there are no expectations. What else can you really strive for in a lost season? There’s no chance at the playoffs barring 11 consecutive wins to end the year and we know that’s not happening. At this point, most of this staff is coaching for their livelihood. Jim Harbaugh is probably safe given that this type of year is an anomaly based on his lengthy and successful resume. Chris O’Leary, barring a massive collapse by the defense (who knows what happens if they end up trading Khalil Mack!), should be safe given how well he’s kept his unit chugging. They’ve been without Derwin James and top cornerback Donte Jackson the past two weeks, on top of missing starting defensive tackle Dalvin Tomlinson and career special-teamer Del’Shawn Phillips starting at inside linebacker. The fan base is fairly split between tanking for a blue-chip prospect or actually turning it around and looking like a competent football team the rest of the way. I don’t see any type of turnaround happening as long as they’re trotting out four rookies on the offensive line. Completely unreal what’s happening up front with the injuries and it’s the second year in a row where only the worst players of the bunch manage to stay healthy. If Jim Harbaugh is worth the pretty penny that he’s getting paid, he’ll prove that this entire situation is a fluke. Fire or hire the right people and get this thing turned around before the 2027 offseason arrives. 2. Justin Herbert has completed 59.4% of his passes for 937 yards, five touchdowns and seven interceptions while being sacked 17 times. What has been the biggest reason for his struggles in Mike McDaniel’s offense? Two big things: 1.) The offensive line has simply been abysmal, and that’s before the injuries really started to take their toll. Check any number from whomever you want, Herbert is getting hit at historic rates and nothing has changed since last season when he was the most hit quarterback in the league. Last time I checked, he was the most-sacked quarterback in the NFL since being drafted in 2020. His best protectors can’t stay healthy and the front office has done a horrendous job at fixing the problem. 2.) After five weeks, I think it’s simply safe to say that McDaniel’s offense does not jive with Herbert or the personnel. It looks like he’s trying to fit square pegs in round holes, and for some reason none of that got ironed out in the preseason. Based on training camp reports and the little bit of preseason snaps we saw among the starters, the offense looked great. It looked very competent. I simply don’t understand what happened between the final preseason game and the season opener against the Cardinals. Herbert looks like he’s simply doing what McDaniel tells him to and throwing to who he is told to throw to, over actually running the offense and having control over the entire show. How do we explain the blatant turnovers thrown into the chests of defenders? How do we explain why some of their best players are off to the worst start of their careers? Nothing makes sense with this team anymore. 3. Despite the winless record, the Chargers’ defense ranks second in defensive success rate and eighth in EPA per play. What has allowed that unit to continue playing well while the offense struggles? The defensive coaching staff under Harbaugh has been very good since it was compiled in 2024. Mike Elston has coached the defensive line well, mainly turning reclamation projects into coveted free agents (s/o Poona Ford and Kristian Fulton). Steve Clinkscale has worked wonders with the young defensive backs. Khalil Mack’s guidance has also been huge for the young pass rushers. Overall, they just look like a unit who understands the mission. They understand their goals and know how to execute the vision of O’Leary. It’s such a stark contrast from the other side of the ball that it’s hard to comprehend. Lastly, how good is this unit that they rank as high as they do even when they’ve started a league-high 18(!) drives inside their own territory. That’s seven more than seconds place! This unit is worth their salt and O’Leary really be one of the best up-and-coming defensive minds right now. 4. The Chargers opened the week with seven players unable to practice and another 13 limited, including Joe Alt, Derwin James, Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnston. Which injured player’s availability would have the greatest effect on Sunday’s matchup? Right now, it’s Joe Alt. The defense has been fine without Derwin James or Donte Jackson. The offense was bad with or without both Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnston. Alt at least gives Justin Herbert one good to great offensive lineman who can protect him. Without him, it’s going to be sixth-round pick Alex Harkey yet again. There’s a chance veteran Daniel Brunskill gets the start, but we won’t know for sure until game day most likely. But let’s be honest, none of those players lifted are enough to really move the needle in this matchup. 5. The Chargers swept Kansas City in two one-score games last season, but they now enter Arrowhead at 0-5 against a rested 4-0 Chiefs team. What is your prediction for how Sunday’s game plays out? I think the Chiefs are going to win by double-digits and maybe actually win in a comfortable manner. The Kansas City defense is also very good this year and if some of these other units can cause the Chargers to turn it over in their own territory multiple times as game, the Chiefs should have no problem doing it the same. It might be a big day for Harrison Butker as this defense still manages to hold teams to 3 over 7 most times, but put their backs to their own goal post enough and anyone would be able to break through for a few more scores than expected. I foresee the Chargers kicking a few field goals but failing to find the end zone even once. My score prediction for this one is 24-9 Kansas City with Justin Herbert once again turning it over more times than touchdown passes thrown.

title: Chiefs-Chargers Week 6 game and score predictions from Arrowhead Pride
summary: It’s time for the Arrowhead Pride staff to put their opinions to the test. Before the Kansas City Chiefs host the Los Angeles Chargers, our writers predicted the final score and result. The Chargers may not have had the “Offseason Champions” accolades they frequently boast entering the season, but few expected an 0-5 start and […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s time for the Arrowhead Pride staff to put their opinions to the test. Before the Kansas City Chiefs host the Los Angeles Chargers , our writers predicted the final score and result. The Chargers may not have had the “Offseason Champions” accolades they frequently boast entering the season, but few expected an 0-5 start and making a case for the NFL’s worst offense. They will try to get their first win on the road against a rested Chiefs squad coming off the bye. FanDuel Sportsbook currently lists Kansas City as 8.5-point home favorites. When last on the field, the Chiefs were tested but came out undefeated against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium in Week 4. We also want to know your score prediction! Vote in the poll on The Feed and share your score prediction ! Jared Sapp ( @TrumanChief ) The Chargers’ 0-5 start is perhaps the season’s biggest development. Still, a division game should always be taken seriously. Yes, it would be easier to name the Chargers not on this week’s injury report than to speculate on who might play through a number of serious ailments. Yes, Mike McDaniel and Jim Harbaugh appear to be from different planets. But I’m going to plan a close game. Even if they play without longtime Travis Kelce nemesis Derwin James, I expect the Chargers defense to do what they’ve done for years: make this an ugly game that comes down to the fourth quarter. I expect Kansas City to come out on top, but I’m planning for a frustrating Sunday afternoon. Chiefs 24, Chargers 20 Caleb James ( @CJScoobs ) I did not expect this to be the season of the Chargers’ undoing, but it has come at a good time for the Chiefs as they work their way back to the top of the AFC. The Chargers swept the Chiefs last season for the first time in nearly a decade, and Mahomes tore his ACL in the game that led to the Chiefs being eliminated from playoff contention. Despite the lopsided record and multiple players out, I still expect both teams to come out with plenty of juice. The Chargers to save their season, but the Chiefs will remind them that the AFC West still runs through Arrowhead Stadium despite the results of last season. Andy Reid off of a Bye Week is always an advantage, and his team will enter the game at nearly full health. With multiple starters out, I expect the Chargers to try to play the clock and play keep-away from Mahomes to help keep themselves in the game. The Chiefs offense will be without their key deep threat, Tyquan Thornton, but the combination of Mahomes and Kenneth Walker should be enough to get past the floundering Chargers. Chiefs 24, Chargers 14 Mark Gunnels ( @MarkAGunnels ) I don’t see the Chiefs having much trouble taking care of business against the Chargers on Sunday. We already know Andy Reid’s track record coming off a bye week, and now he’s facing an 0-5 Chargers team that’s absolutely decimated by injuries. On top of that, Justin Herbert is playing some of the worst football of his career. I expect the Chiefs to come out sharp, handle business, and win this one comfortably. Chiefs 27, Chargers 13 Maurice Elston ( @MrMauriceElston ) The Chargers enter Week 6 at 0-5, making them one of the NFL’s biggest surprises for all the wrong reasons. Justin Herbert and the offense have struggled under new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, although the defense has kept them competitive. Injuries along the offensive line only make things tougher against an undefeated Chiefs team coming off a bye. On paper, Kansas City should win comfortably. But a winless division rival fighting for its season makes this a dangerous matchup. The Chargers would love nothing more than to hand the Chiefs their first loss. I don’t see that happening Sunday. Despite injuries at wide receiver, Kansas City can continue leaning on Kenneth Walker III to keep the offense moving and create opportunities for Patrick Mahomes through play-action. Defensively, this feels like the week “Sack Nation” returns, with the Chiefs taking advantage of a depleted offensive line and making Herbert uncomfortable. Los Angeles will put up a fight, but Andy Reid’s team will leave the bye ready to handle business. Chiefs 30, Chargers 20 Matt Stagner ( @stagdsp ) Your 4-0 Kansas City Chiefs are back to face another division opponent after the bye week. The winless Los Angeles Chargers come to town as the most disappointing team in the league after being a favorite breakout team for approximately 30 straight offseasons. They aren’t untalented but have played poorly. That makes them dangerous at 0-5 with their backs aga the wall. Expect a close, bitter contest between division rivals, regardless of the records. Herbert will probably throw a couple of touchdowns, especially if his top 2WRs were back in the lineup. It’s all going to come down to how well the Chiefs can execute. I expect the pass rush will get 3+ sacks. I expect Walker to have 100 total yards. I don’t know what to expect from the Chiefs receivers. Will Cyrus Allen get a real shot? Will Xavier Worthy produce? Can they make up for injuries to Rice and Thornton? My prediction is that it won’t be pretty, but it will be enough. Chiefs 27, Chargers 24 Dakota Watson ( @D_Watson56 ) Throw the records out for this one. To me, it doesn’t matter the Chiefs are undefeated and the Chargers are winless. Every time these teams play, it seems to be a battle that comes down to the wire. And despite being winless and at times inept, the last three losses for the Chargers have all been by a score. These teams know each other, and I think it will be another close game. I don’t expect a full game from Rashee Rice if he does play, and this leaves the receiver room as a major question mark. Expect a big game from Travis Kelce and for the pass rush to finally get home multiple times against the Chargers’ beat up offensive line. Chiefs 30, Chargers 24 Rocky Magana ( @RockyMagana ) Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh is a franchise vampire. He drains the talent out of an organization and gets as many wins as he can before they shrivel up into a corpse. Unfortunately, the Chargers were already halfway to hospice by the time he took the reins. In the end, Ol’ Khaki Bottle Glasses will pin the Chargers 30th-ranked offense on offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel (AKA The Vape Prince) to buy himself another year. But how is the Chargers 22nd ranked defense Captain E-Cig’s fault? The Chiefs are coming out of the bye. Despite being banged up at wide receiver, as long as they don’t play down to the competition, they should take care of business. Chiefs 36, Chargers 12 Nate Christensen Chiefs-Chargers has been exciting for the past couple of years and had a lot of intrigue coming into the season. That is no longer the case, as the Chargers are 0-5 and a complete train wreck. There’s a good chance the Chargers’ entire staff gets fired. They’re incredibly banged up on offense, and the whole unit seems checked out. Division games can get weird, but with the Chiefs off a bye and the Chargers facing this opponent, I feel like they should easily cruise to a win. Chiefs 27, Chargers 13 Ron Kopp Jr. ( @RonOnChiefs ) When a team is in as much of a down spell as the Chargers are, the Chiefs have no excuse to let them up off the ground. Los Angeles’ incredible injury report, which named more than 20 players on Thursday, reflects how broken the team has looked over five games. Quarterback Justin Herbert hasn’t elevated the team with his own play, so it’s on Kansas City to do what it takes to ensure he doesn’t get a bounce-back performance. That’s what it will take to beat the Chiefs in Arrowhead on Sunday. Off a bye week, the team should relish this opportunity at home and take care of business. Expect defensive tackle Chris Jones to come off a bye week and lead a resurgent pass rush, taking advantage of strong man coverage on the back end to tally multiple sacks on Herbert in an imperfect victory that moves the…

In Week 4, the Chiefs narrowly […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The undefeated (4-0) Kansas City Chiefs will take on the winless Los Angeles Chargers (0-5) on Sunday afternoon. The game will kick off at 3:25 Arrowhead time and will be broadcast locally on CBS ( KCTV-5) . The Chiefs enjoyed an early Week 5 Bye week, undefeated and atop the AFC. In Week 4, the Chiefs narrowly defeated the Las Vegas Raiders 30-27 to remain unbeaten. Despite not playing last week, running back Kenneth Walker is second in the NFL with 537 rushing yards and is on pace for a massive season. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes appears back in MVP form, but he has sustained losses to his receiving corps, with Tyquan Thornton likely out for the season and Rashee Rice slated to miss time with a hamstring injury. Few saw the Chargers’ porous season coming, but they are on the verge of being eliminated from the playoffs before the end of October. The Chargers haven’t lost a game by more than a possession, but an onslaught of injuries and turnover issues have plagued them so far and will linger into this matchup. Here are five things to watch. 1. Receivers stepping up The receiver room took a big hit with Thornton lost for the season, and Rice set to miss time with a soft-tissue injury. While most of the Chiefs media scape is clamoring for outside help, this will give the Chiefs reserve wideouts a chance to show what they can do. Cyrus Allen was the talk of Chiefs camp, but to this point in the season has played sparingly. He has yet to catch a pass and has played only 10 offensive snaps this season. The fifth-round pick out of Cincinnati became a training-camp and preseason darling, showing strong route running and good hands. Cyrus Allen stock 📈👀 pic.twitter.com/z6BROJqIln — FantasyPros (@FantasyPros) August 29, 2026 Second-year player Jalen Royals has seen an uptick in snaps and caught his first career touchdown pass in Week 2 against the Indianapolis Colts. Out of the jumbo look, having WR's line up in line is a great way to free up players in space. With all eyes on Walker and Tonga, Mahomes makes a great run sell and delivers it to Royals in the back of the endzone. pic.twitter.com/EV5OfVf54n — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) October 10, 2026 Royals has seen the field for 23% of the offensive snaps in 2026, but has only caught three passes. The Chiefs signed Justin Watson to the practice squad this week, a reunion that brings back a key member of the back-to-back Super Bowl teams. During his time in Kansas City, Watson caught 42 passes for 785 yards and five touchdowns, and was at his best when going deep. It will be worth monitoring if they activate other practice squad players like Andrew Armstrong or Omari Evans in the coming weeks. The Chiefs could make an outside move before the trade deadline, but they will give their in-house options the first crack. 2. Attacking Herbert Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert is having a horrendous start to the 2026 season. He is tied for the league lead in turnovers with nine two-fumbles and seven interceptions—and ranks low in every major passing category. Herbert has had some great games agaisnt the Chiefs recently, but with a decimated offensive line and below-average receivers, he struggled greatly this season. Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel has not helped the cause, but Herbert’s decision-making has been bad, to say the least. Chargers last 3 drives: Justin Herbert INT Justin Herbert fumble Turnover on downs pic.twitter.com/nWO55R27A5 — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) October 11, 2026 The Chiefs are tied for second in the NFL for turnover takeaway differential at +5 through four games. The Chiefs defense has allowed some points this season, but they have been opportunistic when it comes to taking the ball away, and this week could be a good chance for them to add to their dominance in the takeaway category. In his career against Kansas City, Herbert has 22 touchdowns, seven interceptions, and a 102.9 passer rating. He may be struggling, but the Chiefs defense must bring their A-game to keep him down. 3. Delane and Williams dominance By now, there should be no doubt that general manager Brett Veach can find cornerbacks. A season after trading away All-Pro Trent McDuffie, his replacement, Mansoor Delane, is looking the part in just three career games. Mansoor Delane with one of the GREATEST two-play sequences you’ll see from a rook. Registers a TFL on Ashton Jeanty, and follows it up with CLAMPING Brock Bowers. The Chiefs rookie CB NEUTRALIZING some of the NFL’s top weapons 😳🔒 pic.twitter.com/oHzd3YU6qM — Rookie Watch (@RookieWatxh) October 4, 2026 Delane has been impressive, and his opposite-field counterpart, Nohl Williams, has stepped into his own after a solid rookie season. This is outstanding football by Nohl Williams. Good initial coverage to stick with the WR and take away the outside. When the QB looks to go deep, he sticks side by side with the WR and makes sure to get his head around before knocking away the pass. pic.twitter.com/P2nVGGS6yi — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) October 15, 2026 The Chargers’ two best wideouts, Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnston, are both listed as questionable after missing a week, which could spoil a good matchup against the corners. Both corners have also been strong in run defense and will likely play big roles there this week. 4. Pass rush finishing with sacks The Chiefs pass rush needs to pick it up, and this could be a get-right game for them. Through four games, the Chiefs have recorded only four sacks, tied for least in the NFL, and have been middle of the pack with 39 total pressures. Herbet has been pressured the third most in the NFL—42 times—and sacked the second most, 17 times. The Chargers will play a makeshift offensive line this week, so the Chiefs pass rush must find ways to get home on passing downs, starting up front with the defensive line. KC needs to see more of this out of Woods after the Bye. The return from A-gap to B-gap allows him to use his lateral mobility and quickly get the LG's hands off with a swipe. If not for the RB chipping, he is in the backfield even quicker. pic.twitter.com/ZKhkRqdjXc — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) October 12, 2026 5. The offensive line This is a big week for the Chiefs offensive line in multiple ways. With tackle Josh Simmons practicing in some capacity, he will likely return to the starting five in the coming weeks, leaving either Jaylon Moore or rookie standout Kahlil Benson as the odd man out. A Hi-Five from Patrick Mahomes and more participating in individual drills in Media Watch than Wednesday for Josh Simmons today. #Chiefs pic.twitter.com/mW86J0bAnO — Harold R. Kuntz (@HaroldRKuntz3) October 15, 2026 Another situation to monitor will be the left guard spot. In Week 4 against Las Vegas, Mike Caliendo unexpectedly took a spot start over Kingsley Suamataia, who started every game this season and last season at the position. Reid did not clarify the reason in the press conference, but did mention Suamataia would be back in the mix this week. By all measures, Suamataia has played fine this season, so his absence has been more of a mystery than anything. Overall, the offensive line has played fine this season, and the Chiefs will need them to win this game.

title: The Chiefs need Xavier Worthy now more than ever
summary: Giving up a second-round pick was entirely too much. I know it, you know it, we all know it. That doesn’t make it any less disheartening to see the news over the past week: The Houston Texans traded for Marvin Harrison Jr. The Kansas City Chiefs signed Justin Watson. It’s a tale as old as […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Giving up a second-round pick was entirely too much. I know it, you know it, we all know it. That doesn’t make it any less disheartening to see the news over the past week: The Houston Texans traded for Marvin Harrison Jr. The Kansas City Chiefs signed Justin Watson. It’s a tale as old as time. One AFC team makes a big move while the Chiefs settle for the homecoming with a known commodity. That doesn’t make it the wrong move. It just makes it the convenient one. The Chiefs find themselves in a tough spot at wide receiver again. Tyquan Thornton emerged in the first month of the regular season as the team’s leading receiver. Rashee Rice was finally starting to look more like himself. And then disaster happened. Thornton is out for an extended period of time with a dislocated ankle. We’ll see how long Rice misses with his hamstring issue. The only active wide receiver this week with more than 20 receiving yards on the season is Xavier Worthy. Jalen Royals has played 60 offensive snaps this season. Rookie Cyrus Allen has only played 10. This team needs bodies to fill out the roster. Watson helps them do that. For now. Eventually something else has to give for this offense. Someone has to replace the production Thornton was providing in the deep passing game, in particular. His average target this season was over 18 yards downfield. Only two other wide receivers in the NFL with at least 15 targets have a comparable average depth of target. Neither of them is nearly as productive on those targets. Patrick Mahomes had a 154.9 QB Rating this season when targeting Thornton. A perfect passer rating is 158.3. Those deep targets open up everything underneath — the passing game, the running game. Everything. Thornton was a critical element to the offense. It’s going to be a lot to replace. I didn’t anticipate saying that in 2026 about Tyquan Thornton, but here we are. Marvin Harrison Jr. wasn’t the answer to fill the Tyquan Thornton-sized hole in the offense. Not for the price the Cardinals demanded, at least. I found 23 trades over the past decade that included at least a second-round pick as compensation for a wide receiver. I can only think of two or three instances in which the team that made the trade for the receiver would do it over again if they knew then what they know now — the Philadelphia Eagles trading for A.J. Brown, the Buffalo Bills trading for Stefon Diggs and (possibly) the Dallas Cowboys trading for Amari Cooper. The Texans are pretty likely to regret this deal. They had to make it given their situation: a quarterback nearing the end of his rookie deal and the reality of what faces a team after a 1-4 start. Desperate times call for desperate measures, and this reeks of a desperate move. The Chiefs could feel more urgency to make a significant move within the next month. The trade deadline is November 10th. That means only four games remain before it’s decision time. The clock is ticking, and one player is under particular pressure. It’s time for Xavier Worthy to step up. ⏰⏰ @XavierWorthy https://t.co/bBmZo8b23u — Patrick Mahomes II (@PatrickMahomes) October 6, 2026 If anyone on this roster can replace some of what Thornton brought to the table, it’s Worthy. He has the deep speed. We’ve seen him make contested deep catches before. Remember his catch against the Bills in the playoffs? Where’s that receiver been this year? Worthy’s 1.05 yards per route run this season ranks ahead of only Kayshon Boutte, Isaiah Williams, Ted Hurst, Rashid Shaheed, Quentin Johnston, Chris Bell, Darnell Mooney, Courtland Sutton, Makai Lemon, Jerry Jeudy, Marvin Harrison Jr. (!!!), Bryce Lance and Jauan Jennings among wide receivers who have run at least 100 routes this year, per Sumer Sports . His 6 yards per target this season is the eighth lowest among all wide receivers with at least 20 targets. We could go on, but we’ve discussed this before. It’s not good. Worthy has been on the field more than ever this season, but less productive than ever. I don’t know if it’s an issue with his role, getting comfortable on the field again after his injuries last year, or what. But… it’s time for him to step up again. If Worthy can regain the form he found at the end of 2024, the Chiefs won’t have an issue at receiver. He finished with 58 receptions on 76 targets for 679 yards and 6 touchdowns in the final seven regular-season and three postseason games that year. That’s a 17-game pace of 99 receptions for 1,150 yards and 10 touchdowns. That’s a legitimate No. 2 wide receiver, exactly what the team is lacking. If he can’t regain that form, another move will be necessary. Options are limited. A player like Jeudy from the Cleveland Browns makes some sense. Quentin Johnston isn’t overly inspiring, but he’s the kind of deep threat this team could use. Let’s hope the Chiefs never have to explore that path. The best-case scenario for everyone involved is for Worthy to come out of the bye with something to prove and remind everyone why the Chiefs selected him in the first round a couple of years ago. This team can win a Super Bowl. They can’t let the receiver position drag them down again.
