title: Patriots mailbag: How can Drake Maye attack the Jets?
summary: The New England Patriots are looking to keep their winning streak alive as they welcome the New York Jets to Gillette Stadium. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. How would you attack the Jets defense? – Maye The Force Be With You What’s different about the Jets this year that would help them […]
full_text: The New England Patriots are looking to keep their winning streak alive as they welcome the New York Jets to Gillette Stadium. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. How would you attack the Jets defense? – Maye The Force Be With You What’s different about the Jets this year that would help them avoid another drubbing like they got at the end of last year? – paulnewman As he did with his defenses in Detroit, Jets head coach Aaron Glenn wants his defense to play man coverage and blitz. Through the season, New York ranks second in blitz rate and 10th in man coverage rate. However, that approach could be costly against Drake Maye, who has excelled against the blitz and can exploit man coverage by pushing the ball downfield or making plays with his legs. If the Jets lean heavily on single-high coverages, expect Maye to take his shots, as he did last week. The most notable change for the Jets this season has been Glenn’s increased versatility on defense. New York is leaning more heavily into split-safety coverages, including a significant increase in Cover 6, and could feature those looks Sunday to limit Maye’s deep-ball opportunities. While there isn’t much to fear from the Jets’ offense from this perspective with Christian Gonzalez available to limit Garrett Wilson, New York has also overhauled its defensive personnel this offseason, potentially setting the stage for a low-scoring divisional battle. Rookie David Bailey has gotten off to a fast start on the edge, while veteran safety Minkah Fitzpatrick is still making plays in the backend. With Henderson being out a few weeks, how do you see the offense compensating for that? More Stevens, Corey Kiner increased load, or perhaps getting our younger WR’s more involved by adding more 4-5 WR sets & spreading out opposing D’s? – KissBillsRings With Henderson out for sometime, could we see Larison called up? – jpd985 We’ll see if Henderson misses time after somehow logging a pair of limited practices this week. If he’s out Sunday, Rhamondre Stevenson should be expected to carry the load, as he did in the regular-season opener when he played 60 snaps with Henderson sidelined. Behind Stevenson, Larison would likely be elevated from the practice squad again, as he was in Week 1, with Kiner handling the change-of-pace carries. While the fumble is something a depth running back can’t afford, I thought Kiner actually ran well against the Raiders last week. If Yahoo’s stats are right, the Pats are 11th in the league in rushing yards/game at 121.6, and 16th in the league in rushing yards/attempt at 4.1yd/att. So they’re persistent? With Gilliam and Henderson laid up, and a Jets team begging for jumbo packages running down their throat to wear down their talented defensive line, what do the Pats have to do to improve rushing efficiency? – WannaBe Pats GM More of what they’ve done the last two weeks. After a slow start on the ground this season, the Patriots have changed things up and become less predictable scheme wise. They’ve spiced up their go-to ground game with more motion and window dressing and have leaned into new schemes as well. With much being written about how Maye couldn’t handle the 2 high safety looks from last year’s playoffs and the first few games of this season, what has changed? Did BUF and LV not play those looks or have worse personnel? Or are there signs that Maye is starting to handle that better? – Palm_Fronds_and_Shamrocks Maye ranked near the top of the league in several metrics against Cover 2 last regular season. However, given his exceptional deep-ball efficiency, it was — and still is — viewed as one of the best strategies for limiting explosive plays. The issues in the playoffs seemed to stem more from the quality of opposing defenses than from the schemes themselves. Maye hasn’t had many issues against those coverages in recent weeks, although it was puzzling to see Las Vegas opt for the opposite strategy and play single-high man coverage on more than 50% of its drop backs — a risky approach against a quarterback like Maye. Were you excited to finally see the Patriots use Pop Douglas & Kyle Williams correctly against the Raiders leading to 3 TD’s and 156 Yards combined? – For Pats Sake The usage didn’t really change for DeMario Douglas and Kyle Williams last week. Douglas scored two touchdowns against busted coverages and ran a pair of really strong routes. Williams, meanwhile, finally got opportunities to make plays downfield against a Las Vegas defense that played single-high safety on more than 50% of its snaps. He capitalized. Considering the injury bug that hit our team until now, who would be the 8 IR players you think should be brought back during the regular season? What about the extra two players, after we go into the playoffs? Would you wait with the last 2-3 spots closer to the playoffs to see if a certain position needs more help than others (say CB instead of WR)? – Maxxwell This is something the Patriots will have to manage moving forward when it comes to their roster. They have already used two return designations on Marcus Bryant and Brenden Schooler, with A.J. Brown set to take the third. Of the remaining players on injured reserve, Mack Hollins and Reggie Gilliam should be considered likely candidates for two more spots. From there, the Patriots can remain flexible with the final three regular-season return designations, plus two additional spots in the playoffs, as no other player on IR appears to be an immediate priority to return. That’s all for this week’s #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you’d liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post on the Feed. Make sure to follow @iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.

title: A.J. Brown brings ‘fresh juice’ to Patriots offense
summary: After spending the designated four weeks on injured reserve with a high ankle sprain he suffered in Week 1, New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown has been cleared for practice. He did not participate fully on Wednesday or Thursday, though, making his status for Sunday against the New York Jets uncertain. Still, offensive coordinator […]
full_text: After spending the designated four weeks on injured reserve with a high ankle sprain he suffered in Week 1, New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown has been cleared for practice. He did not participate fully on Wednesday or Thursday, though, making his status for Sunday against the New York Jets uncertain. Still, offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels noted how it was “good to see him back out on the practice field,” and that Brown returning could provide a “fresh juice” to the guys in the wide out room. “This happens quite a bit for us,” he said. “You miss a guy for a week, two weeks, sometimes longer than that, and then you have an opportunity to get him back during the course of the season, it’s always good. It brings some fresh juice to the guys and to the unit. We know what he can do when he’s out there and he’s healthy. We’ll see how the rest of this week goes and ultimately what ends up happening.” The Patriots have gotten inconsistent production from the top of the receiver group in Brown’s absence. This may be partly because there isn’t a weapon that demands extra attention or has the same presence as him. Since Brown hasn’t played much this season, McDaniels doesn’t have much data to describe how the offense changes with him in it. But he compared it to the way Stefon Diggs drew attention in 2025 against the Jets. “Last year they doubled Diggs in the Jet game a couple times,” said McDaniels. “So, anytime they put two people on one person, then someone else has a single opportunity.” As good as it would be for Drake Maye and the New England offense to get their top target back as soon as this Sunday, it was made clear that it was no guarantee from the Patriots’ medical team. McDaniels was asked about having Brown back, which he quickly corrected to “when” they get him back, definitively showing that there is still an argument that Brown is not ready to go yet. Brown himself said that his status is “still up in the air” and that it is “a coach Vrabel decision” on if he steps on the field for the first time since the third quarter of the season opener against Seattle.

full_text: STARKVILLE, MISSISSIPPI - OCTOBER 25: Kelley Jones #1 of the Mississippi State Bulldogs intercepts a pass during the first half against the Texas Longhorns at Davis Wade Stadium on October 25, 2025 in Starkville, Mississippi. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images The way the season is going for the Saints, all things are possible for this roster at this moment. So, when you’re watching college football games this weekend, here are a few players to watch, regardless of their position. Carter Smith is an offensive tackle who plays at Indiana, and with the way the offensive line has performed, it wouldn’t be a surprise if that’s where the Saints choose to make another investment. Smith is one of the best, and he will be taking on a really good edge rusher in Kenyatta Jackson, who plays for Ohio State. That game will be at 11 a.m. on Fox. Smith is currently ranked as the fifth-best offensive tackle on Mel Kiper’s Big Board. Smith has played against Jackson before, including in the 2025 Big Ten Championship Game, which the Hoosiers won 13-10. The Saints obviously need to have a true number-one corner, and Kelley Jones could be him. Jones plays for Mississippi State, and the Bulldogs will be playing the Tigers in Baton Rouge at 11 a.m. on ESPN. So far this season, Jones has allowed a completion percentage of only 28%. He is a true outside corner with size and range and is a consensus first-round selection. Jones will be tested by the LSU offense. The Tigers feature several talented receivers and one of the best passing offenses in the nation. If Jones can hold his own, he could help the defense take away one side of the field and make containing the LSU offense more manageable. Another edge rusher who is not getting a lot of headlines but is currently viewed as a first-rounder is Yhonzae Pierre. Pierre is currently ranked as the third-best edge rusher in the 2027 class. So far this season, Pierre has 2.5 sacks, 17 tackles, one interception, and a forced fumble. The Tide will be taking on the Volunteers at 2:30 p.m. on ABC. Pierre is going to be tested by the Volunteers, but not just in the passing game. Tennessee will be featuring DeSean Bishop, who is having an amazing season, especially with the uncertainty at the QB position. Bishop just ran for 138 yards on 19 carries against Arkansas, and the week prior, he ran for over 200 yards. If Pierre can hold his own against the run and play a complete game on the edge, it could get ugly in Knoxville for the Volunteers. What position group would you like to see the Saints address? What players are you watching this weekend? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Saints Draft Position: Entering Week 6
summary: The bad teams in the NFL are remaining bad, and unfortunately, the New Orleans Saints are one of them. Even with the loss against the Minnesota Vikings, the Saints’ draft position did not change, so I wanted to look at the second round this week. As of now, the Saints are selecting 38th, and here […]
full_text: COLUMBIA, MO - OCTOBER 10: Cayden Green #70 of the Missouri Tigers prepares to block in the third quarter of an SEC football game between the Texas A&M Aggies and Missouri Tigers on Oct 10, 2026 at Memorial Stadium in Columbia, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The bad teams in the NFL are remaining bad, and unfortunately, the New Orleans Saints are one of them. Even with the loss against the Minnesota Vikings, the Saints’ draft position did not change, so I wanted to look at the second round this week. As of now, the Saints are selecting 38th, and here are two prospects the Saints could select: Missouri OL Cayden Green There has been so much investment in the offensive line, but it’s still not enough. I do think this group is underperforming due to coaching. The Saints have 4 high-level offensive linemen (including the injured Bansk Jr.) that have proven in the past how good they are, and it’s too early to say their struggles are because of skill rather than coaching. It’s similar to the 2024 Saints defensive line. But that one spot that can still be upgraded is RG, and although Jeremiah Wright has potential to take over, the second round would be a great place to just get a starter. The top option on the board is Missouri offensive lineman Cayden Green. For Missouri, Green has been a long-time starter since transferring in 2024, and he has played both guard and tackle. Turning 22 this year, Green is still young and has space to improve, but he’s not developmental. He’s a powerful blocker who can move anyone he goes up against. His strength (no pun intended) is his pass blocking, but his run blocking is also very good. BYU RB LJ Martin The Saints just signed Travis Etienne Jr. to a multi-year contract, and selecting another RB in the draft is by no means a replacement move. New Orleans’ run game is poor and although coaching and injuries have contributed, it’s also clear the Saints are missing a powerful runner. CJ Donaldson has been the best option so far, but he hasn’t shown enough to be RB2 next season, and Etienne has played better with a physical running back that complements his skills. This class is mostly undersized, elusive, and fast running backs, but in the second round, LJ Martin fits what the Saints need. He can gain tough yards; he’s quick, has great vision, can change direction to find that space, and is super patient.

full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - NOVEMBER 12: Chris Olave #12 of the New Orleans Saints catches a touchdown pass against the Minnesota Vikings during the third quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium on November 12, 2023 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) This week, the New Orleans Saints will face the New York Giants in Week in 6 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Ed Valentine of Big Blue View joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: Do you expect newly acquired QB J.J. McCarthy to see the field at any point this season, or has Jameis Winston done enough to establish himself as the starter for the remainder of the year? EV: McCarthy already has seen the field. The Giants have a ‘McCarthy Package’ that they used for the first time last Sunday against the Commanders. I expect we will continue to see that. As for the rest of the year, I couldn’t tell you. Teammates love and respect Jameis, and are happy playing for and with him. That said, John Harbaugh is not going to sit back and do nothing if Winston plays poorly and the season starts to go sideways. Right now, Winston is playing well enough and the Giants are doing well enough no change will be made anytime soon. Can I guarantee Winston will start for the remainder of the year? No. NJ: Who are some notable names who will be sidelined for the Giants on Sunday against the Saints? Is there a particular area in which New Orleans could exploit? EV: Well, of course QB Jaxson Dart and edge defender Brian Burns are out for the year. Right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor and edge defender Abdul Carter, both with calf injuries, could miss Sunday. Carter is the Giants’ best defender and pass rusher, and he would be sorely missed. NJ: If you could take one player off the Saints’ roster and put him in the Giants’ lineup, who would it be? Why? EV: Chris Olave. That’s easy. Put Olave with Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely, and the Giants would be in the conversation for the best trio of pass catchers in the NFL. The Giants need more explosive plays, and adding another star receiver to the mix would help get them. NJ: Who is one Giants player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Sunday—someone who may not receive much national attention but could have a strong performance? EV: If you haven’t been paying attention to the Giants, I think you will be surprised how much of the passing attack runs through tight end Isaiah Likely. He was a backup for the Baltimore Ravens. He joined John Harbaugh with the Giants, and he is becoming a star. He is second in the league among tight ends with 33 receptions, second in target share, and fourth in receiving yards. NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Saints (-112) are currently 1.5-point favorites over the Giants (+104) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction and how do you see the game playing out? EV: In our weekly picks, I took the Giants. They are simply finding ways to play through their mistakes, and Harbaugh has them believing they have earned the right to win and to be a good team. Problem is, if Carter doesn’t play, that is a huge problem for New York. He is the driving force in their pass rush, and they wouldn’t be the same defense without him. title: Our Defense vs. Their Offense: New York Giants
summary: The Saints’ defense will be out to prove everyone wrong this Sunday as they prepare to take on Jameis Winston and the New York Giants’ offense. The Giants are without starting quarterback Jaxson Dart due to a season-ending knee injury. Even without Dart, the Giants still have some weapons they will look to feature against […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Carl Granderson #96 and Chase Young #99 of the New Orleans Saints stand on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Saints’ defense will be out to prove everyone wrong this Sunday as they prepare to take on Jameis Winston and the New York Giants’ offense. The Giants are without starting quarterback Jaxson Dart due to a season-ending knee injury. Even without Dart, the Giants still have some weapons they will look to feature against a defense that presents several favorable matchups. This is not a very explosive offense. The Giants currently rank 21st in total offense, averaging 308 yards per game, while the Saints allow 362 yards per game, which ranks 26th in the league. The Giants are averaging only 199 passing yards per game, ranking 20th, and 109 rushing yards per game, ranking 16th. The Saints’ passing defense comes in ranked 13th overall, allowing 212 yards per game, but their rushing defense is a putrid 31st, allowing 150 yards per game. This is a game where the Giants will more than likely look to feature Cam Skattebo. Skattebo has not really been able to get the ground game going. His best rushing performance so far came in Week 1 against the Cowboys, when he carried the ball 18 times for 81 yards and one touchdown. This matchup against the Giants feels very similar to the Vikings game. It’s another team with offensive struggles, and those struggles fall directly into the areas where the Saints’ defense has struggled. The obvious answer would be that the Saints need to stop the run and force the Giants to pass the ball. They need to get New York into obvious passing situations by keeping the offense off schedule. The only issue with that is the Giants still have Malik Nabers as their primary wide receiver. If New York looks to get Nabers involved early and often, that could create problems for this Saints secondary. Saying that this Saints defense is struggling would be a massive understatement. They have moments when they look good and moments when they are absolutely horrible. In a game like this, the Saints will need to force Jameis Winston to be the guy who beats them. And if Jameis is on his game, that creates an even bigger problem for the defense. Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy will look to establish the run to set up the rest of his offensive philosophy, which features more of a West Coast-style passing attack. The Saints will have to do something they have not been able to do consistently all season, and that is stop the run. Keep the Giants behind the chains, and don’t let Nagy get rolling by implementing the quick passing game on top of an efficient, on-schedule rushing attack. The Saints will also have to find a way to generate pressure. The Giants have allowed 13 sacks so far this season and have thrown three interceptions. Meanwhile, the Saints have recorded 10 sacks and only one interception, but they have recovered four fumbles. Right now, the Giants are 3-1-1, and looking at their statistics, you can tell they have won a lot of ugly games. But at this point, Who Dat Nation would gladly swap situations with the Giants. The Saints are going to have to step up on Sunday and create some offense for themselves by forcing turnovers in this road matchup. This game should be a fun one to watch, especially considering what Mrs. Benson had to say a few days ago. The defense needs to come out, establish its aggressiveness, and shut down the Giants’ offense on the very first drive. What do you think about the Saints’ defense matching up against the Giants’ offense? Do you think one team has an advantage, and if so, what is it? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: New York Giants mailbag: Cam Skattebo, ‘peanut punch’, more questions
summary: Robert Stolzenberger asks: A lot has been made, rightfully, about the Commanders’ poor deciding and executing at the end of OT in game 5. But wouldn’t it have been much safer and smarter for the Giants to have tried the field goal on 2nd down (I think it was) instead of handing it off to […]
full_text: Robert Stolzenberger asks: A lot has been made, rightfully, about the Commanders’ poor deciding and executing at the end of OT in game 5. But wouldn’t it have been much safer and smarter for the Giants to have tried the field goal on 2nd down (I think it was) instead of handing it off to Skattebo for a couple of more yards up the middle? They were already inside the 25 yard line and any score would have won the game immediately. Winston had been on fire and the Washington defense was pretty grabby already on every play. Seems to me I recall Parcells and other team’s coaches not waiting for 4th down or taking more time off the clock in similar situations — rather just get it over with. Also, who would make that call, the OC or Harbaugh? We should be 4-1. Ed says: Robert, no. Stay with me, and I will explain. Skattebo ran for 5 yards and a first down right before the overtime two-minute warning. So, what you are asking is if the Giants should have simply kicked the field goal on first down coming out of the two-minute warning. Now, of course if the Giants make the kick there they win the game, Both teams had already possessed the ball once. But … there is always a’but’. Remember that placekicker Dominic Zvada missed three of five field-goal tries in the game, and had already missed from 46 yards during overtime. Washington had already used its two allotted timeouts in overtime. Yes, if you make the kick there you win the game. If you miss, though, you are handing the ball to Washington at about the 32-yard line with 1:50 to play. They have plenty of time to go down the field and kick a game-winning field goal, even without timeouts. We saw that play out. Had the Commanders not screwed up the clock management they moved down the field after the fumble and had plenty of time to get off a makeable field-goal try. The idea is to run the ball twice, maybe three times and work the clock down so that the game-winning field goal try by Zvada would be the final play of the game. That way, you take away any chance Washington has of winning the game. Here is how Harbaugh explained it Sunday night: “The idea was to run it twice, and then run it down, get as close as we could, protect the football, which we talked about numerous times, and then run it down and take the knee. So in case he doesn’t make the field goal, there’s no time for them to come back and get the field goal. That’s the strategy.” It was absolutely the proper way to play the situation. If Skattebo does his job, the Giants leave the Commanders with no opportunity to win. The only other way to do it is to take a knee three straight times, but that does result in moving the ball back a bit. Peter Calamari asks: I wonder jf anyone says a connection between the deterioration of the Giants running game and the substitution of Hudson for Schmitz at center. It seems like since that switch was made the Giants are running much less effectively although possibly pass blocking somewhat better. Ed says: Peter, it’s not the move to Bryan Hudson at center in place of John Michael Schmitz. Hudson has been better than Schmitz. If you judge by Pro Football Focus grades, which isn’t always the best way to judge, Hudson has been about 30 points better as both a run- and pass-blocker. The difference is adjusting to a run game where the big difference-maker was supposed to be Jaxson Dart’s mobility. Dart’s Week 1 22-yard run is still the longest of the season for the Giants. Without the threat of the quarterback run game, the Giants are much more predictable and limited on the ground. Neither Cam Skattebo nor Najee Harris are guys who can outrun NFL defenders or possess enough wiggle to make defenders miss. The blocking has to be perfect, and with teams loading up the box and outnumbering the Giants at the line of scrimmage it hasn’t been. Another thing that doesn’t help is Andrew Thomas’s groin injury. He is clearly laboring to get through games, and while he is playing well, he isn’t playing as well as a healthy Thomas is capable of. Peter Smyth asks: I’m wondering about the “punch” play that Washington used to get Skattebo to fumble in OT and used on Likely’s second TD (didn’t count as a fumble). I guess I’ve never noticed a defensive player just standing there and making no attempt at a tackle, just waiting, watching the ball, then punching it as the guy goes down. My questions: How to protect against this play? Are the Giants doing this to other teams? Has this been going on for years and I’m just noticing it? Isn’t this on the head coach to prevent? It must work a lot if they are trying it. Interested in your thoughts. Ed says: Peter, I am not crazy about the play. It is legal, though, and has been around for a while. It does seem to be becoming more of a thing in recent years. Yes, the Giants do it to other teams. Jevon Holland is good at it. I have seen Arvell Reese try to do it. It is becoming standard practice when one defender has a player under control for the next defender to try and punh the ball out. Tell me what a head coach is supposed to do about it. If a runner has the ball securely in two hands with a good grip on it and a defender punches the ball in the right spot with enough force it is going to come out. Maybe the smartest thing a runner can do is realize when it’s time to stop fighting for six more inches and get to the ground before somebody knocks the ball out. Bob Donnelly asks: With Sunday’s tie the NY Giants are in first place in the NFC East and, with a .700 winning percentage (3.5 /5), have the third best record in the NFC. Could you please share the scenarios of how, at the conclusion of the 18 game season, a tie helps/hurts a team? Ed says: Bob, tie games count as a half-win and half-loss. So, let’s say the Giants and Eagles both finish with nine wins atop the NFC East. The Eagles, unless they also tie a game this season, would be 9-8. The Giants would be 9-7-1. The way the NFL looks at ties, they would technically be 9.5-7.5, so they would have the better record and would be division champs. This played out in 2022. The Giants were 9-7-1. They made the playoffs as a wildcard. The 9-8 Detroit Lions went home without a playoff berth. Right now, there is no way to know what all of the scenarios will look like at the end of the year. ctscan123 asks: Hey Ed, I do not understand any resistance whatsoever to J.J. McCarthy being a Giant. I don’t see how it could be considered anything less than a slam dunk. It’s a fifth-round pick for a quarterback drafted 10th overall who missed his entire rookie season due to injury and started only 10 games in his second year. The expectation that young quarterbacks should make the leap from college to the NFL and immediately hit the ground running is bordering on ridiculous. If he develops into a starting quarterback, whether for us or for another team after we’ve developed him, it’s an absolute steal in terms of trade value. If he becomes a competent backup, it’s still a good deal. And for those keeping track, regardless of whether he blossoms and supplants Winston, we do actually need a backup quarterback this year. If he fails, you’ve lost a fifth-round pick. For Pete sake, what is the hit rate on fifth round picks in the NFL? I’m not much of a gambler, but isn’t this deal basically all upside? What am I missing here? I know this is a rant disguised as a question which is one of your favorite things, but the opposition to this move is one of the bigger head-scratchers I’ve encountered in a long time. Ed says: CT, where are you reading about resistance to the McCarthy trade? I have not seen much resistance to the trade itself, but everyone is entitled to his or her own feelings about whether or not the Giants should have done it. I wasn’t crazy about giving up a fifth-round pick, but the Giants felt he was the best quarterback available at the time and that the price was reasonable. There are people who will argue the Giants simply should have…

title: Giants vs. Saints matchup: How will New York attack the New Orleans defense?
summary: The 3-1-1 New York Giants host the 1-4 New Orleans Saints, who are -1.5 favorites with a 45.5-point Over/Under. The Giants have covered the spread in the last two weeks, but Vegas isn’t fully buying the Giants’ recent success. The Saints have faced a difficult schedule: The Saints almost pulled off an epic come-from-behind upset […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo | Getty Images The 3-1-1 New York Giants host the 1-4 New Orleans Saints, who are -1.5 favorites with a 45.5-point Over/Under. The Giants have covered the spread in the last two weeks, but Vegas isn’t fully buying the Giants’ recent success. The Saints have faced a difficult schedule: Past strength of schedule, future strength of schedule and a TON more here 🔽 https://t.co/qIy7vTgQa5 pic.twitter.com/tYqotQKnvi — PFF (@PFF) October 13, 2026 The Saints almost pulled off an epic come-from-behind upset victory in Week 1 at Detroit before pulling off the upset in Week 2 at Baltimore. However, they’ve lost three straight games at home against the Raiders, Falcons, and Vikings, with a combined score of 103-64. Quarterback Tyler Shough threw for 96 yards against Brian Flores’ defense last week and he struggled against Atlanta in Week 4, but the second-year signal caller was solid through the first three games. However, the Saints defense has played very poorly through five weeks. With that, let’s look at that Saints defense. The Saints defense Former Chargers’ head coach Brandon Staley coordinates the defense. The Saints allow the second most points against with a high 30.2 points per game. They surrendered the seventh most yards per game – 371 yards. Their run defense has struggled; they allow 148.8 yards per game (second most) and a league-high ten total rushing touchdowns. The Robinsons of the Falcons – Bijan and Brian – ran all over them in their building two weeks ago. New Orleans’ pass defense ranks 20th in yards against ( 213.4 yards per game ). New Orleans’ defense ranks 27th in turnover percentage forced, and they have ten sacks on the season, which ranks in the middle of the league. The Saints allow a touchdown on 63.6% of their red zone trips (20th in the NFL), and they’re 29th in the NFL in third-down conversion rate, with a concerningly high 48.3% rate. The Saints blitz at a 31.8% rate, which ranks ninth most in the NFL, with an 18.2% pressure rate, which ranks 29th in the league. New Orleans uses middle-of-the-field closed at a 71% rate, with a lot of Cover-3. Their nickel 2-4-5 package is their most used, and they are a base 3-4 team. Teams have done well to attack the right side of their defense with the run. The Saints’ defense has played poorly through five weeks, but former Washington first-round pick, Chase Young, has turned his career around in New Orleans. The 27-year-old has 20 pressures and four sacks on the season; we should see a good Young vs. Andrew Thomas matchup on Sunday – throwback! Carl Granderson mans the other EDGE position. He has eight pressures and 2.5-sacks on the season. Veteran Cam Jordan is playing in the twilight of his career; he pressured Kyler Murray twice last week and has six pressures on the season. Anfernee Jennings missed the last two games with a knee injury, but he is the fourth rotational EDGE. Chris Rumph II and Tyree Wilson may see snaps on the EDGE as well. Colby Wooden and Khristian Boyd are the starting defensive tackles, but New Orleans have rotated their defensive line quite a bit this season. They lost Bryan Breese in training camp and Nathan Shepherd missed last week with an injury, but has seven pressures on the season. Davon Godchaux hurt his groin in Week 4 but played 18 snaps in Week 5; he has played 125 total snaps this season. Vernon Broughton has provided some pass rush juice to the defensive line; he has six pressures on the season. Rookie Christen Miller returned to the lineup in Week 5 and played 28 snaps. Veteran John Ridgeway plays a depth role as well. Overall, the defensive line is a work in progress that has lost more than they’ve won in 2026. Second-year linebacker and former Oklahoma Sooner Danny Stutsman has started the last two games with Kaden Ellis injured, and he’s played well. He is second on the team in STOPs behind Chase Young. Stutsman joins Pete Werner, who is a quality starting linebacker in the league. The defense uses three safety looks often in their nickel packages, but Kool-Aid McKinstry and Quincy Riley are the starting cornerbacks on the outside. The former has allowed a 60.7% completion rate with three passes knocked away, while the latter allows a 56.5% catch rate with two PBU. Martin Emerson Jr. is the third outside cornerback. Safety Jonas Sanker plays slot cornerback for the Saints. He has surrendered two touchdowns with a very high 88.9% completion rate. Sanker is, however, one of the better tacklers in space and he operates well around the line of scrimmage. Justin Reid and Julian Blackmon are the Saints two starting veteran safeties. THE MATCHUP The Giants are in an interesting position against the Saints, who struggle to stop the run. New York wants to be a heavy personnel, under center, team; the Giants have used 22% at a 20% rate this season, 21 personnel at a 15% rate and 12 personnel at a 19% rate. They often use 13 personnel too with Chris Manhertz, Isaiah Likely, and Theo Johnson. Heavier personnel usually means a run first to play action team, but the Giants have struggled early in the last two games when they leaned on this approach. However, the best of Jameis Winston was unlocked once the Giants transitioned to spreading the offense out and attacking out of the shot-gun. It wasn’t always out of 11 personnel, though, the Giants have went EMPTY out of 13 and 12 personnel over the last two weeks, and it’s led to their best personnel usage per EPA. The Giants will likely attempt to attack the Saints on the ground, specifically the right side of the defense, but I would like to see New York move to a more under center approach earlier if they can’t establish the run. The Giants were down 14-3 and 27-13 over the past two weeks, and successful offense was sparked through the shot-gun Jameis Winston approach, so Matt Nagy and Greg Roman should incorporate those concepts earlier. McKinstry and Malik Nabers are familiar with one another, and the latter can win that matchup. Neither of the linebackers are a good match for Isaiah Likely, who could see a lot of Sanker in the slot; Likely should be fine uncovering against this defensive personnel. A hefty target share of Nabers and Likely should remain. Malachi Fields was open several times deep last week, as Dan Quinn focused adjacent zones on Malik Nabers. If Staley utilizes a similar approach, New York should look to take a deep shot to Fields, who will see a lot of Quincy Riley. Designed touches for Mooney aren’t the only way to get him involved in the offense. Similar to Fields, Mooney uncovers often on deeper concepts, and a deep shot could be dialed up for the 28 year old receiver. The Giants running back situation is a big topic of conversation. Cam Skattebo is splitting time with Najee Harris and Tyrone Tracy Jr. Skattebo’s devastating fumble that cost the Giants a win in overtime will not help his case. Skattebo still led the room with a 63% snap rate, but Najee Harris had an 18% snap rate with Tracy Jr. playing 19% of the snaps. Tracy Jr. has earned the third down role, and Skattebo disappears for stretches of the game. I don’t love the rotation. Despite the fumble, I would like to see Skattebo more, and I would also like to see Devin Singletary active instead of Harris. The Giants ground game has been abysmal since Week 1. There’s a solid argument that Singletary has the best vision of the backs. If Nagy wants to roll with three backs, I do hope to see Singletary over Harris, although the former Pittsburgh Steelers physical running style seems to fit the identity that the Giants’ are still trying to establish and impose on opponents. One question on the offensive line – should the Giants continue to start Bryan Hudson? I think Hudson has played better than John Michael Schmitz. Is it substantially better? No, I wouldn’t say that, but the former UDFA seems to be more controlled with slightly more pop on contact. I ask this, though, because Francis Mauigoa played his worst two…

full_text: Darius Slayton | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Former New York Giants wide receiver Darius Slayton has been released by the Indianapolis Colts, the team announced Friday morning . After seven seasons with the Giants, the 2019 fifth-round selection, was released by the team a week before the season began. Slayton signed with the Colts, where his former Giants teammate Daniel Jones is the starting quarterback, on Sept. 22. Indianapolis had hoped Slayton could provide a deep threat after an injury to Alec Pierce. That never materialized. The 29-year-old never played a snap for the Colts. Slayton suffered a knee injury that kept him out of the Colts’ lineup in Week 5. Now, he is again looking for a new team. Slayton caught 296 passes for 4,435 yards in seven seasons with the Giants. He was slowed last season, when he had 37 catches for 538 yards, by double sports hernias for which he had surgery in the offseason.

title: The Jameis Winston experience: What it means to his Giants teammates
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The Jameis Winston experience. The New York Giants are living it full-throttle right now, with Winston starting in place of the injured Jaxson Dart as quarterback of the NFC East-leading Giants. What, though, is the Jameis Winston experience? To some, it is the wildly entertaining, erratic, up-and-down play Winston has been […]
full_text: Jameis Winston EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The Jameis Winston experience . The New York Giants are living it full-throttle right now, with Winston starting in place of the injured Jaxson Dart as quarterback of the NFC East-leading Giants. What, though, is the Jameis Winston experience? To some, it is the wildly entertaining, erratic, up-and-down play Winston has been famous for throughout his 12-year career. No other quarterback has a 30-touchdown, 30-interception, 5,000 passing yards season on his resume. Winston is must-watch TV. To some, it is the larger-than-life personality that came through the TV screen when he worked as a correspondent during the World Cup, or shows up whenever Winston has a microphone or camera in front of his face. To his Giants teammates, though, the Jameis Winston experience is something different. ‘A man of increase’ We should start with how Winston himself views the Jameis Winston experience. He was asked on Wednesday what the phrase means to him. “My take on the Jameis Winston experience is that I am called to be the light of the world and the salt of the earth, right? Every time that I’m around someone, I am driven to increase that man or that woman with every action that I take,” Winston said. “So, if you’re defining that as the Jameis Winston experience, I’m telling you that is the Jameis Winston experience that I intend to give. “Now, all the other perceptions, again, (former Washington quarterback) Joe Theismann, man, he told me once perception is reality. So, people can say whatever they want to say. But my intention is to be a man of increase. Increase in every man, every woman that I come in contact with, doing onto them as I would want them to do onto me.” ‘I love talking about him’ Backup quarterback J.J. McCarthy is one of Winston’s newest teammates. He arrived via trade from the Minnesota Vikings just three weeks ago. “I love talking about him,” McCarthy said when I asked McCarthy for a couple minutes of his time on Thursday. “My experience with Jameis has been something I’m extremely grateful for because he leads by example as well as leads vocally. “When he talks about wanting to increase the next man or woman beside him, that is so real. He wants to do everything he can to help. Extremely unselfish. Has this unique way of thinking and talking about football that is such a well-rounded, polished version of somebody that’s been around so many great minds and has had so many great experiences. “Just being able to watch him prep, watch his routine throughout the week, be with him while he’s doing his routine. I’m already picking up so many things that I’m adding to mine.” McCarthy gave ‘Kudos’ to Winston for going above and beyond to help him learn the Giants’ offense as quickly as possible. I asked him for an example. “Just going over front structure and linebacker identification. I had no idea,” McCarthy said. “Everyone talks about how they see the defense in different ways. We’re going into Week 5. He’s starting. He doesn’t have to be walking me through all that stuff where it’s just basic, general information about our offense. “But, he gets up on the board and talks me through everything, like 30-40 minutes.” McCarthy has also noticed how Winston interacts with teammates. He told a story from his first day with the Giants, calling it “a beautiful tonesetter.” “My first day here in the unit meeting we were watching the Tennessee game and him and Isaiah Likely just had this unbelievable, mature conversation that I’ve never been a part of, where everyone is talking about I saw it this way, I saw it this way, and then just being able to get on the same page,” McCarthy said. The Winston fans don’t see Likely calls the phrase Jameis Winston experience “kind of insulting in a way.” “Jameis is a great quarterback,” Likely said. “I mean, I feel like in the second half [vs. Washington], you guys [saw] exactly what Jameis is capable of doing in this league, and the offense is capable of doing as well.” Winston remained out on the field while Likely was speaking to media on Thursday doing extra work post-practice. Likely spoke about the Winston that fans and casual observers don’t see. “They don’t see Jameis after practice, throwing with whoever needs extra work catching the football. They don’t see him talking about each and every route when the defense is out there for their rack of plays. They don’t see when Leek [Malik Nabers] obviously is tired, him bend down and tie Leek’s cleat in the middle of the game, when he’s tired as well, he has to look at the protections, everything about that,” Likely said. “They don’t see how hard he is practicing in OTAs, training camp and everything, et cetera. I mean, obviously, they’re going to see what he posts, what the world posts about him, trying to be a goofy guy. But, at the end of the day, he’s a quarterback in National Football League. He’s there for a reason.” Cam Skattebo also lauded Winston’s work ethic. “He works hard. He works his ass off,” Skattebo said. “He’s probably still on the field right now. It’s been 30 minutes, 20 minutes after practice. He’s just a guy that works hard, continues to put everything on the table for us. When you have somebody like that at quarterback you can stand behind it and give it your best shot and give it everything you have because you know he’s gonna give that to you.” ‘Unbelievable teammate’ One of those players Winston has gone out of his way to help is wide receiver/kick returner Charlie Jones, who was claimed on waivers by the Giants just before the start of the season. “I think the Jameis Winston experience, you’re gonna get everything, but you’re gonna get a guy who comes in here every day giving his very best,” Jones said. “He’s an unbelievable teammate. He’s just genuine. You see him on social media is exactly how he is in person. “Before I got here all I knew was his social media clips, and he’s just like that.” Jones, though, has also learned how Winston leads and how serious he is about football. “He’s someone that holds you accountable. Just a great teammate. Someone you learn from every day as a player and as a man,” Jones said. Like McCarthy, Jones is a player who has benefitted from Winston’s willingness to give teammates his time. “I’m out there every day with him,” Jones said. “Making sure he gets what he needs, then if I need something at the end I ask him for that, too. “Consistent. So consistent every day. And will hold people accountable if he sees someone not being consistent. Not just to say something, but because he genuinely cares about the guys in the room, and the guys in the building.” ‘All business’ Veteran tight end Chris Manhertz said the Jameis Winston experience is “pretty damn good to me.” “The football player is all business,” Manhertz said. “The football player is extremely detailed, he’s diligent in his process. More importantly the way that he communicates with us as an offensive individually is somebody that wants to be aligned in everything we do collectively as an offense. “Off the field is off the field, but once we come in this building it’s all business to try to get a win.” In the Giants locker room, that is all they can ask for.
author: Ed Valentine

title: Giants’ DC Dennard Wilson: ‘We like playing with a chip on our shoulder’
summary: The New York Giants are 3-1-1 and in the driver’s seat of the NFC East. They might not have won in Week 5, but they also didn’t lose and still managed to expand their lead in the division by half a game. While the story of Week 1 as the Giants’ suffocating offense, the story […]
full_text: New York Giants linebacker Arvell Reese sacks Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New York Giants are 3-1-1 and in the driver’s seat of the NFC East. They might not have won in Week 5, but they also didn’t lose and still managed to expand their lead in the division by half a game. While the story of Week 1 as the Giants’ suffocating offense, the story of the last three games has been the defense. The Giants have been led by defense over the last 7 quarters, with Dennard Wilson switching to an aggressive blitzing front. The Giants now lead the NFL in Cover-0 (pure man coverage across the board) and are second in the NFL in in blitz rate over the last two weeks. Their defense has been impressive and it’s been leading to wins — the Giants haven’t lost since starting quarterback Jaxson Dart was lost for the season. Yet for the third game in a row, the NFC East leading Giants are underdogs against a cellar-dweller. And much of the national media is once again is picking the Giants’ opponents over the division leader. “Everybody counts us out,” defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson said Thursday. “We like playing with a chip on our shoulder. That’s what it is.” On the Giants’ blitzing attack The Giants made a significant adjustment in the second quarter against the Arizona Cardinals and it was a minor revolution for the defense. The Giants had spent the first 13 quarters of the season relying on their athletic edge defenders to win on their own, and not blitzing often. After the Cardinals carved them up in the first quarter of Week 3, the Giants started sending pressure and it changed their entire defense. “It’s been effective,” Wilson said. “I mean, we’ve been able to hit the quarterback. We’ve been able to disguise. They don’t know where it’s coming from. And the biggest thing when you pressure, the DB’s are covering well so you have more confidence in calling it. They’ve been doing a good job on the back end, communicating, playing man-to-man, playing fire zone coverage. So, it’s been good for us. It’s been effective and we’ve been getting the quarterback off the spot and forcing them to bad decisions.” It’s almost a surprise that the Giants waited as long as they did to unleash their blitz package. Perhaps the weather slowed them down against the Tennessee Titans, but Wilson certainly seems happy to be blitzing now. “I like everybody blitzing,” Wilson said. “On our defense, everybody’s a blitzer. Dru is a dynamic player. Dru, let’s talk a little bit about [CB] Dru (Phillips) and his growth. Dru has been playing some really good, high-level football the last three or four weeks in coverage, blitzing, playing the run. He’s ahead of things. I love where he’s at, but he is an asset. He is an explosive, he’s another violent player that’s not afraid of contact. And when we get the opportunity to send him or any other player that we have, we work on it, we rep it, and they go full speed and you don’t know where it’s going to come from.” “One thing I like about this group, they love going forward,” he added. “They love attacking. So, they all are attack players. So, in our scheme, we have the ability to run blitzes from everywhere and anybody can come from different looks. And that’s the enjoyment of being in this system, running this system, and also the players fitting within the system. So, they can come from anywhere.” In particular, the Giants’ blitzes have unleashed rookie linebacker Arvell Reese, who has quickly become one of the most dynamic defenders in the NFL. For his part, Wilson relishes the opportunities to get Reese going forward and matched up on smaller blockers. “If you can get Arvell on a running back, it’s a good matchup for us any day of the week,” Wilson said. “He is a violent scud missile. When he goes forward, I say he’s like a bull, he’s sees red and it’s good for us. If we can dictate and get a running back and get him on a one-on-one, more times than not he’s going to win. And if the first time that he goes, he’s going to make you feel him. And if he can make you feel him and then he’s already elusive and a hell of an athlete, so now they can set him up with moves and things like that. So, it’s always fun to turn on the film and see Arvell when he makes contact with people because it doesn’t look good.” On the defense against the Washington Commanders The Giants were generally very good against the Washington Commanders, but they had a couple lapses. In particular were the two long scrambles by QB Jayden Daniels. Wilson said Thursday that neither play should have happened. “Well, first and foremost, both of them (QB Jayden Daniels’ runs) should never have happened,” Wilson said. “We had a five-man front with a game, and we didn’t execute the game. And when we didn’t execute the game, we didn’t have a guy wrap. And if the guy wrapped, he would have been right in his face. And then on the second one, it’s about balancing the rush. You can’t have two interior tackles outside of the hash. And we didn’t get vertical penetration, and he got out. Both situations, the one on the first touchdown, it was a second and six, right? And we always talk about you can spy, and we had a spy in the game but on second down, are you spying when you’re really trying to go pressure them there? But for us, in the run game and with the quarterback scrambling, it’s about our execution. It’s about everybody doing their job when their number’s called. The first run that popped should have never popped either. They had we call a plunge play with the tight end going back, and we had three guys behind the ball. When that happens and they flash back, the three guys got to work in unison to rock back, and we didn’t. And that starts from communication. That starts from eye discipline. That’s being ahead of the play, but we’ll get that fixed. And for the most part, we’ve been pretty good at it but we can’t have those lapses. And we’ve been communicating with the players a lot about this. It’s like if you just do your job and don’t worry about anything else and you take care of your responsibility, we play really good defense. When one guy gets out of whack, this or that, things happen. Also on those plays, we got to get them down in the secondary. And ultimately if things pop, we got to get them down in the secondary. But we worked diligently this week just making sure our communication is loud, it’s obnoxious, it’s annoying, and making sure that we surround the ball this week going into this game.” Daniels’ two touchdowns were mistakes by the Giants, and the offense would have done more than enough (eventually) to win if the defense had shut Daniels down. But for the third game in a row, the defense ultimately made the play to win (or at least not-lose) the game. In this case, Wilson credited Kayvon Thibodeaux and Darius Alexander for heads-up plays to slow the Commanders down and burn the closing seconds of overtime. “Well, I think it all goes back to the whole unit with the situational awareness,” Wilson said. “Harbs (John Harbaugh) does a great job, and we’ve been in that situation before in practice, that we’ve practiced that and how to handle it. But let’s go back to that play, I mean, without Thibs (edge defender Kayvon Thibodeaux) making that play and forcing the quarterback to go down when he added to him, that play wouldn’t have happened. So, it’s just kudos to all of them. (DL) Darius (Alexander) was very good on that play too, trying to hold things up. So, it was a lot of situational awareness there and obviously, I wish we got it done before that instead of having a tie. But the guys, they bowed up in that fourth quarter. They didn’t waver. They attacked the moment from everybody on defense. And I just love their tenacity and the way they know how to finish. “The key for us is just to execute,” he added, “to communicate, get the call, get aligned, beat them into a stance, and then line up and play our style of…

title: NY Giants news: Abdul Carter injury, Cam Skattebo talks about his fumble, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants prepare to battle the New Orleans Saints on Sunday. Bring on the blitz! Changing the identity of the Giants’ defense | ESPN.com This week’s opponent could bring a different approach as the Giants take on the New Orleans […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants prepare to battle the New Orleans Saints on Sunday. Bring on the blitz! Changing the identity of the Giants ’ defense | ESPN.com This week’s opponent could bring a different approach as the Giants take on the New Orleans Saints on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, Fox). Saints QB Tyler Shough has been just a touch above average against the blitz, with a 0.1% completion percentage above expectation (CPOE). He has five touchdown passes and two interceptions against the blitz. Wilson’s track record doesn’t show a heavy lean on the blitz. His Titans defense blitzed just 22.8% of dropbacks over the previous two seasons, the 22nd-highest rate. He sent DB blitzes 9.3% of dropbacks, which was 25th over that span. Perhaps that changes a bit with the Giants short-handed on pass rushers. It might be the best way for them to survive. Giants embracing the underdog role Dennard Wilson was asked about the Giants being underdogs against the Saints: "Everybody counts us out. We like playing with a chip on our shoulder." pic.twitter.com/FssaD8qvwG — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) October 15, 2026 Giants adamant Kayvon Thibodeaux is making a bigger impact than modest stats indicate | New York Post Sunday was almost a homecoming game for Kayvon Thibodeaux. The Saints called the Giants about trading for Thibodeaux during April’s draft but found the asking price — believed to be a third-round pick — too high. Watching from afar as reports surfaced, including from The Post, Thibodeaux posted an image from “Fast & Furious” to social media with the tagline, “You thought you could leave without saying goodbye.” Jameis Winston ’ s starting dream is alive as the Giants roll into a game against the Saints | FOX Sports When Jameis Winston signed with the New Orleans Saints in 2020 initially to back up Drew Brees and then to be in the mix to succeed him at quarterback, he was long removed from winning the Heisman Trophy in college and being the top pick in the draft. He did not give up on being a starter in the NFL again, like he was early in his career with Tampa Bay. “I dreamt of it,” Winston said. “And now it’s here.” Giants WR reveals details of intense exchange with Jameis Winston: ‘You know how to read lips?’ | NJ.com Winston wanted Mooney to flush the drop and refocus — echoing what Mooney had told Winston in the wake of his own mistakes. Said Mooney: “That was his opportunity to tell me, ‘As much as you tell me to f— it, this is my time to tell you: F— it. It’s OK. Just move on. I’m coming back to you right now.’” It wasn’t just the drop that had Mooney annoyed in that moment when it appeared he was rolling his eyes at Winston. In reality, Mooney said, he was aggravated about how the afternoon had unfolded. “It was just how the game was going for me,” he said. “I got face masked. I got poked in the eye. When I had a ball, I got ran into, and I thought it was a [pass interference]. It’s just that things weren’t going well for me.” ‘Big, fast, physical ’ Giants tight end emerges as special teams playmaker | The Record Theo Johnson entered the NFL harboring dreams of becoming one of the league’s top tight ends. The former New York Giants coaching staff used to show him highlights of Rob Gronkowski, pulling him out of meetings to bring him upstairs, just to break down Gronkowski video for inspiration and motivation. Now in his third season, Johnson isn’t giving up on that goal just yet. Confident Giants kicker Dominic Zvada: ‘If nothing has changed, nothing should change’ | New York Daily News Zvada said he spent Monday dissecting what went wrong and now has no need for a rear-view mirror as he prepares for the New Orleans Saints. A return to MetLife Stadium and to a turf field might help his footing, and he is no less confident than he was last week. “I really just try and focus on what I can control,” he said. “That’s kind of how I’ve been able to have success early in the season is by just focusing on not the score or where we’re at in the game or anything like that. It’s just focused on going out there, having that mental checklist in my head and lining up and kicking the ball through the uprights. That’s really all I need to focus on. I’m kind of just forcing myself to focus on that, and when you force yourself to focus on that, everything else just kind of fades out. And then you’re just kind of in your own world. So it’s nice.” New York Giants ’ John Harbaugh: Isaiah Likely a ‘ unique kind of athlete ’ | USAToday.com “When he was being evaluated, he went in the fourth round; I think it was late fourth round. Nobody really could get their arms around him. He made all these plays in college, but it just looked different. You see it out here, it turns out it’s really good what he does,” Harbaugh said. “He’s elusive; he can get away in man and zone coverage. He’s got a great feel; he’s got great hands, he has an amazing catch radius. He’s an elusive runner, a good, strong runner. So, all those things that are football. He’s also, and this was in college, he was crazy good as a perimeter blocker. He would launch guys through the air, like five yards through the air sometimes at Coastal. He’s a really good perimeter blocker here too. He’s translated really well, and I think he’s been able to really express that here this year. The kind of player he is, and it’s just great to see.” From Big Blue View Abdul Carter held out of practice for 2nd straight day ‘Peanut punch’ prevalence has gotten Giants’ attention 5 takeaways from Matt Nagy: Good things coming in Giants’ running game? title: Previewing the Jets’ opposition: New England Patriots
summary: The New York Jets find themselves in a familiar position heading into Sunday’s game in New England. If they could just find a way to upset the Patriots, it change the direction of their season and start to see them considered as a force to be reckoned with in the AFC. Could this be the […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - DECEMBER 28: Rhamondre Stevenson #38 of the New England Patriots runs with the ball against the New York Jets during the first quarter at MetLife Stadium on December 28, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Pamela Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New York Jets find themselves in a familiar position heading into Sunday’s game in New England. If they could just find a way to upset the Patriots, it change the direction of their season and start to see them considered as a force to be reckoned with in the AFC. Could this be the time when they finally achieve that, or will they be hanging on to relevance by a thread once again after Sunday? Let’s break down the Patriots’ roster going position by position: Quarterbacks Drake Maye is coming off a season where he was a legitimate MVP candidate. However, after three weeks, he wasn’t playing like that. The Patriots were 1-2 as Maye had thrown six interceptions and just one touchdown pass. However, he’s rediscovered himself over the past two games, leading New England to a come-from-behind win against the Bills and a blowout of the Raiders. His 374 yard output against the Raiders represented the second-highest total of his career, as he completed multiple deep balls. Over the two wins, he had seven touchdowns and just one interception. The Patriots’ number two is Tommy DeVito, who won three straight games as an undrafted rookie with the Giants but hasn’t had much success since then. Seventh round rookie Behren Morton is the number three. Offensive Line New England has a question mark on their offensive line this week after left tackle Will Campbell was injured and knocked out of the previous game. Campbell has been practicing on a limited basis all week but his game status is uncertain and he’s listed as questionable. In last week’s game, first round pick Caleb Lomu stepped in for Campbell and did well. In college, Lomu faced David Bailey and handled him well, although this was while Bailey was still at Stanford, so he hadn’t fully broken out yet. New England has multiple ex-Jets on their offensive line with Morgan Moses at right tackle and Alijah Vera-Tucker at left guard. They also have Greg Van Roten, but he’s on injured reserve. The 35-year old Moses is doing a solid job, although he does have five penalties in five games. So far, the injury-prone Vera-Tucker has been completely healthy with the Patriots. The other starters are last year’s third round pick Jared Wilson at center and veteran Mike Onwenu at right guard. However, Onwenu is also on injured reserve, so Ben Brown is currently starting there. Matt Pryor, Walter Rouse and sixth round rookie Dametrious Crownover are available as cover. Rouse already had to fill in for 41 snaps in week three. In the event of an injury to Wilson, Brown would probably slide across to center. Running Backs Similar to Campbell, running back TreVeyon Henderson has practiced on a limited basis this week but his status is uncertain after he picked up a high ankle sprain in last week’s game. He has said he feels pretty good but has been listed as questionable with New England also perhaps thinking ahead to their matchup with the Bears next Thursday. Henderson had 900 yards and nine touchdowns last year, but Rhamondre Stevenson is a more than adequate replacement, who has been a thousand-yard back in the past. He leads the team in rushing yards so far this year. The number three is Corey Kiner, who saw some playing time last week but fumbled once. Pass catchers The Patriots activated AJ Brown for practice this week, after he had been injured in the opener, so he may return to give their offense a further boost on Sunday, although his official game status is questionable. In Brown’s absence, Mack Hollins had been leading the team in receptions, but he is also now on injured reserve. Offseason signing Romeo Doubs leads the team with 219 receiving yards and Pop Douglas is coming off a game last week where he caught two touchdown passes. Slot receiver Efton Chism is now a regular part of the rotation and responded with the winning touchdown against the Bills on a spectacular one-handed catch. Kyle Williams also gets regular playing time and has been established as a big play threat. At tight end, Hunter Henry is off to a modest start, having caught 60 passes with seven touchdowns last year. Third round rookie Eli Raridon is the number two, and has eight catches with a touchdown, while Tanner Arkin and Cameron Latu are also on the roster with Julian Hill on injured reserve. Defensive Line The starters on the defensive line are former first round pick Christian Barmore, nose tackle Cory Durden and last year’s big money signing Milton Williams, who had 3.5 sacks. DaQuan Jones gives them an experienced backup at the nose tackle position with Joshua Farmer and ex-Jet Leonard Taylor III also on the team. All six of these players were active in the Raiders game, although Taylor has played the least on defense. Linebackers New England are without their top two pass rushers from last season, as K’Lavon Chaisson left during the offseason and Harold Landry is on the PUP list. These two combined for 16 sacks last season. In their place, the starters on the edge are Elijah Ponder and Dre’Mont Jones, with Ponder having really stepped up so far as he has 4.5 sacks and leads the team in quarterback hits and tackles for loss. Second round rookie Gabe Jacas is likely to see his role continue to expand though, as he’s flashed playmaking abilities as a rotational player with 1.5 sacks, an interception, three tackles for loss and five quarterback hits. The inside linebackers are led by Robert Spillane, who had 97 tackles last season and is leading the team again in that category. Alongside him, Christian Elliss also plays a full time role. Elliss is another Patriots player who is listed as questionable, although he practiced full on Friday. The reserves on the inside are Erick Hunter, Darius Muasau and sixth round rookie Namdi Obiazor, although they don’t play much. All three got some valuable reps in garbage time last week though. Defensive Backs New England has some real talent at cornerback with their three starters all having posted double digits for passes defensed last year. Former first round pick Christian Gonzalez was a pro bowler and the slot cornerback Marcus Jones intercepted three passes last year to prove he’s not just a punt returner. Carlton Davis was a big money signing who slotted well into the rotation. Davis has been ruled out due to injury and Gonzalez also had some injury issues, but he appears to be good to go. The main backup is Charles Woods, so he may need to step in for Davis. Fifth round rookie Karon Prunty, Channing Canada and Kindle Vildor are the other backups, but Prunty has been ruled out and Canada is listed as questionable. At safety New England brought in Kevin Byard to replace Jaylinn Hawkins, who had led them with four interceptions in 2025. Craig Woodson returns as the other starter with Dell Pettus on injured reserve. Woodson is also listed as questionable but was not limited in practice on Friday, so should be fine to play. Jaylen Reed has also started one game and seen action in three-safety sets, while Mike Brown is available in reserve and Brenden Schooler is mostly just a special teamer. Special Teams Kicker Andy Borregales missed seven kicks last season and has already missed two this year. He had the game winner against the Bills last season and also had the game-winner against Denver in the AFC title game, albeit in the third quarter. Punter Brian Baringer is on injured reserve so veteran Mitch Wishnowsky currently has this role. He has a net average of below 40 yards but has only allowed 64 return yards. In the return game, Jones is a two-time all pro as a punt returner and once had the game winning score against the Jets (albeit due to an obvious missed holding penalty). title: Geno Smith Appreciation Post
summary: As someone who prides himself on objective analysis, it’s equally important for me to acknowledge the highs, no matter how rare they are, in addition to the many lows that come with being a New York Jets fan. I’ll be the first to admit I was very underwhelmed with the Geno Smith acquisition – I […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 27: Geno Smith #7 of the New York Jets reacts to call against the Detroit Lions during the fourth quarter at Ford Field on September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images As someone who prides himself on objective analysis, it’s equally important for me to acknowledge the highs, no matter how rare they are, in addition to the many lows that come with being a New York Jets fan. I’ll be the first to admit I was very underwhelmed with the Geno Smith acquisition – I understood the huge financial benefit of having a starting-caliber QB under contract for $3.3 million but had no belief in Geno in 2026. I didn’t even believe in him from 2013-2016. His Seattle Seahawks days were cool, but even his last year there started to look ugly until he went to Vegas and the wheels completely fell off. No QB in the NFL threw more interceptions from 2024-2025 than Eugene Cyril Smith. 15 in 2024 (2nd in the NFL), 17 in 2025 (1st in the NFL), I thought we were in for another brutal showing at quarterback this year. Boy, was I wrong. Only three quarterbacks this season have started every game this season and thrown zero interceptions: Jared Goff, CJ Stroud, and Geno Smith. After being the most prolific thrower of interceptions for two years, Geno has done a masterful job of avoiding throwing into harm’s way. In fact, he’s become the second passer this century to lead the league in interceptions and then have zero interceptions in his first five games the next year. I dug deep into ESPN.com to discover that fact – only Vinny Testaverde was able to do this, in 2001, after throwing 25(!) picks in 2000. Still, he got his first interception in Week 6 and ended the 2001 season with 14. Geno has six touchdowns and zero picks after five weeks just like Vinny did, but I’m not sure if this middle-of-the-pack New England defense has what it takes to pick him off. I’m thinking Geno might’ve actually turned over a new leaf. This isn’t to say he’s been perfect: he’s fumbled in four of the five games so far, and only four players in the league have lost more fumbles than Geno this season. He looks more “gun-shy” than normal this year, which has led him to hold on to the ball longer behind an offensive line that hasn’t lived up to expectations so far. But I promise this is an appreciation post , so that’s where my criticism ends! Geno’s avoided interceptions, and he’s put Garrett Wilson on pace for the best season of his career by a large margin. Garrett’s current pace is set for 105 catches, 1,271 yards, and 10 touchdowns this year – all of these numbers would break his previous career bests of 101 catches, 1,104 yards, and 7 touchdowns, which all came in 2024 with Aaron Rodgers slinging the ball. Smith’s numbers aren’t quite on pace to beat Rodgers, but you could argue his conditions have been less than ideal. We’ve only seen one drive of the Jets offense at full strength with the original trio of Wilson, Adonai Mitchell, and Omar Cooper Jr. on the field at the same time. We’re still unsure of when that will happen, as Mitchell works his way back from a somewhat mysterious finger injury that required surgery. Geno has also played 40% of his games in the rain, which is a less-than-ideal condition for pass-happy offenses. The Jets defense gets all the credit for holding opposing pass offenses under 200 yards during these games, but the Jets pass offense has also suffered from the precipitation. What would this offense look like with sunny skies, all the wide receivers healthy, Breece Hall healthy, and the confident Kenyon Sadiq who broke out against the Lions? It may be a few weeks until we find out, but Geno has done a superb job steadying the ship in the meantime. For me to enter this season as one of his biggest detractors, I cannot stress enough how impressed I am with this start and how hopeful I am for the rest of the season with him at the helm. Now the idea of having him start in 2027 with a young first-round pick QB learning behind him is starting to sound more like a dream than a nightmare. Let’s go, Geno!

summary: Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense.
