title: A look back at some of the 49ers’ biggest midseason trades under Kyle Shanahan
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have a knack for making blockbuster trades midseason. The odds are even higher when they have a good team and a “missing piece” to put them over the edge. 2026 carries a certain caveat: the 49ers are injured, but they expect a good majority of their players back. That leads us […]
full_text: Oct 31, 2017; Santa Clara, CA, USA; San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch (left) and quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo (middle) and head coach Kyle Shanahan (right) speak during a press conference at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Stan Szeto-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The San Francisco 49ers have a knack for making blockbuster trades midseason. The odds are even higher when they have a good team and a “missing piece” to put them over the edge. 2026 carries a certain caveat: the 49ers are injured, but they expect a good majority of their players back. That leads us to wonder what piece they would actually need , knowing most of their players aren’t out for the season. The trade deadline isn’t until November 10, but that won’t stop the speculating. Rather than make guesses, it seemed like a good time to look back at some of the midseason trades the Shanahan regime made over the years. This won’t be every midseason trade of the 49ers, but it will be a few of the notable ones. Jimmy Garoppolo Year Acquired: 2017 From: New England Patriots Cost: Second-round pick Final Year on the Roster: 2022 Some have a bit of a revisionist history when it comes to Jimmy Garoppolo’s time with the 49ers. Acts like stepping out of bounds during a scramble or being counted on to throw a boneheaded interception just about every game. The thing is, Jimmy G was actually seen as the future at one point, and he backed it up. Garoppolo was drafted by the New England Patriots in the second round of the 2014 NFL draft and served as Tom Brady’s backup. It was widely believed Garoppolo’s pick was seen as the heir apparent. In 2016, Garoppolo filled in for a suspended Tom Brady after the Deflategate suspensions and looked very impressive in his 1.5 games until getting injured (this is going to be a running theme). It was only a game and a half, but it was a good game and a half. Things heated up in 2017, with numerous teams like the Cleveland Browns coming up as possible destinations, but the Patriots wouldn’t trade him. Then on that fateful Halloween day, the 49ers made a move for Garoppolo. Their quarterback room wasn’t impressive, containing Brian Hoyer and a rookie C.J. Beathard—who was starting in place of the ineffective Hoyer. It was almost certain Kyle Shanahan would get then-Washington Commanders quarterback Kirk Cousins the following offseason once the team was done using franchise tags to keep him from leaving the organization. Garoppolo was seen as an alternative if that didn’t happen, and at best a quick rental to see what he could do. A quarterback coming in midseason as a starter is usually a bad idea, especially when Garoppolo is going from the Erhardt-Perkins system the Patriots ran to the West Coast terminology Kyle Shanahan used. Week 12 sped that up when CJ Beathard got injured in the final minute of a home game against the Seattle Seahawks. The 49ers were done at this point; the score was 24-6, and they just wanted to get out of there with little injuries. In that minute, the possibilities of Garoppolo were put on full display: the perfect QB sneak, the quick release, and some Jimmy G magic : a touchdown as time expired. The 49ers went to 1-10 following the loss, but didn’t lose another game that season. Despite his inexperience, Garoppolo offered some of the best quarterback play the 49ers had seen in years. He signed a record-breaking deal in the offseason and finally, FINALLY, the quarterback position was figured out. Kirk Cousins was an afterthought, though some stirred the pot, thinking the 49ers might still find a way to get him. Then in Week 3 of 2018, Garoppolo tore his ACL. The 49ers turned in another losing season. Garoppolo returned in 2019, but something was off—though you didn’t really notice it because the 49ers were delivering a season no one expected, one that had a trip to the Super Bowl waiting for them. With a rookie Deebo Samuel and an acquired Emmanuel Sanders (we’ll get to him), Garoppolo had a powerful offense to work with. Looking back, you almost want to ask if the 49ers were winning despite Garoppolo. You knew something was up in the NFC Championship Game when Garoppolo threw only eight times. Back then, the simple argument was that the 49ers’ run game was so good there was no reason to throw. Looking back, there might have been a deeper reason. In the Super Bowl, Garoppolo had a chance to win the game, but overthrew Sanders as the 49ers blew a 10-point lead. While Garoppolo wasn’t a bad quarterback, the way he played in that game, after all the money the 49ers gave him two years earlier, brought a big microscope. It wasn’t an immediate benching, but he was paid to win games like that or at least give a better effort. Garoppolo battled injuries for the rest of his time with the 49ers. The organization traded three draft picks in 2021 to draft Trey Lance, though Garoppolo was still under contract. It’s all good Garoppolo still started that season, but Lance stepped in when Garoppolo suffered an injury or two. When 2022 training camp began and Garoppolo remained on the roster, everyone knew it was a matter of time before he was off the roster. Moving on was almost a certainty (with him even telling the fans goodbye in the final game of the previous season), but that Trey Lance pick wasn’t looking so hot, so they kept Garoppolo on as the backup. Lance had an ankle injury in Week 2, and Garoppolo was the starter again. Then Garoppolo got a foot injury, and the 49ers went to their third quarterback. Some kid named Brock Purdy. The Jimmy G saga was officially over following the 2022 season. If that’s a lot about a single pick, it’s because that’s how exhausting Garoppolo—and the arguments for and against him—was at quarterback. When he started, he looked like the franchise player the 49ers were missing. Unfortunately, after his ACL tear, a statue would have made quicker movements. While he might not have been one of the best quarterbacks in 49ers history, I do think he was one of the most important. That touchdown against Seattle was more than just a garbage-time score. It signaled what was coming with Kyle Shanahan. It would be a few years until the 49ers lucked into Brock Purdy, and until then, Garoppolo made the 49ers competitive. He darn-near won them a Super Bowl. This is one of those trades that was well worth both the pick and the deal that followed in Garoppolo’s salary. Record-breaking, sure, but the 49ers won with Garoppolo. And they weren’t winning with anyone else under center (despite what some may say). Emmanuel Sanders Year Acquired: 2019 From: Denver Broncos Cost: Third and fourth-round picks Final Year on the Roster: 2019 The 49ers had just about everything. They had a filthy defense helmed by Nick Bosa and DeForest Buckner; they had a decent running game with Matt Breida (and later Raheem Mostert); the wide receivers were a bit iffy. Dante Pettis was a bit of a reach, Kendrick Bourne was more a third-down receiver, and Marquise Goodwin was fast, but his getting injured was a matter of “when.” Enter Sanders. While he debuted against the Carolina Panthers and was mostly quiet, his second game against the Arizona Cardinals showed you this was a good pickup: 112 yards receiving, a touchdown, and immediate rapport with Garoppolo. Sanders gave the wide receiver group a shot in the arm and had instant trust from the quarterback. Unfortunately, while Sanders earned his quarterback’s trust, the quarterback failed to connect on a crucial deep pass that could have altered the NFL as we know it. Sanders left in the offseason and signed with the New Orleans Saints. A classic definition of a “rental,” the 49ers’ passing game would have had deeper issues in 2019 without him. Christian McCaffrey Year Acquired: 2022 From: Carolina Panthers Cost: Second, third, and fourth-round pick Final Year on the Roster: Still on the team After the 49ers had a brutal loss to the Atlanta Falcons, Kyle Shanahan decided to…

Even if he doesn’t practice, he’ll still suit up on game day. Defensive tackle Gracen Halton missed a second straight day with […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - DECEMBER 23: Khalil Mack #52 of the Chicago Bears rushes the quarterback against the San Francisco 49ers during their NFL game at Levi's Stadium on December 23, 2018 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Robert Reiners/Getty Images) | Getty Images 49ers injury updates: Kyle Juszczyk practices in full; 2 rookies miss “Wide receiver Mike Evans didn’t practice for the second day in a row. This is likely how it’ll be with Evans this year. Even if he doesn’t practice, he’ll still suit up on game day. Defensive tackle Gracen Halton missed a second straight day with a quad injury. That’s suboptimal, given the injuries at the position. The 49ers are as thin as you can be at the position. The silver lining is that James Thompson was listed as limited, although that’s not a 1-for-1 swap. Rookie Romello Height was a new addition after practicing in full on Thursday. Height’s designation is an illness, so the hope is that he’s fine, with the game still 72 hours away.” 49ers’ John Lynch says he’s shopping before NFL trade deadline; Kittle asks about Khalil Mack (paywall) “When asked on KNBR on Friday morning about the 49ers possibly trading for Mack, 35, Lynch said “a lot of people ask me that” before revealing Kittle posed the question Thursday. “It’s usually Kittle because he asks about everything, which I love,” Lynch said….“I just like to chirp him and ask what he’s interested in and see if he’ll give me anything,” Kittle said. “So he didn’t really give me a lot yesterday. But me, (fullback Kyle Juszczyk), (left tackle) Trent (Williams), we’ll chirp him just to see if he’ll actually tell us anything. I think he tells Trent the most. Not me, though.” Examining the 49ers’ early-season feat: Generating pressure without Nick Bosa (paywall) “This year, Osa Odighizuwa already has 15 pressures after just five games while rookie Gracen Halton has seven. Odighizuwa’s 12.8 percent pass rush win rate ranks 12th at his position among those who have played five games. Halton’s is 9.6 percent, a rate Odighizuwa says ought to climb as Halton, a fourth-round pick, continues to improve his technique. Halton missed Thursday’s practice with a quadriceps injury. “He’s very raw now,” Odighizuwa said. “So you’re just seeing nothing but upside when you’re watching him play. So it’s exciting stuff.” John Lynch states 49ers trade discussions have ramped up ahead of deadline “Just because the flow of the trade deadline is approaching, yes,” he said. “That’s our job to do that, to talk with our counterparts around the league. We receive calls, we make calls, just to see where the market is at.” Raheem Morris, Klay Kubiak, Brock Purdy share updates ahead of 49ers-Commanders “It was a lot of fun. I’ll give you a quick story. I remember people asking me, ‘How was it coaching [former NFL WR] Julio Jones?’ I said, ‘It’s easy. Good catch, Julio’ (laughter). No, all joking aside, you were able to take your defensive analysis and bring it to those guys while you were learning how to be a good offensive coach and the detail and everything that’s required. That goes into scoring touchdowns and staying on the field and manufacturing first downs. Being around Kyle that first year on offense, it was really the philosophy of what we’re trying to do on football games and how we’re going to go out there and attack people. I had so much fun being able to be over there with the likes of Kyle Shanahan, [Green Bay Packers head coach] Matt LaFleur, [Arizona Cardinals head coach] Mike LaFleur was on that staff, [Los Angeles Chargers offensive coordinator] Mike McDaniel. It was a bunch of really great coaches that were teaching me the backend. And in the frontend, you had all the guys on the front end like [assistant head coach/offensive line coach] Chris Foerster and those guys just teaching you what it was like in the run game and what the rules were and everything that was required to go out there and accomplish what we wanted to get accomplished. You can’t help but bring that back to defense when you had to go back over there. So, when I was able to go back and really formulate how I see the game, how I feel the game, how you want to make your players feel the game, that philosophy really helped me a lot to grow. I think everything from the beginning was really helpful for me when it came to offensive football.” 49ers Week 5 Trench Grades: The duality of it all (paywall) “This week was defined by Gracen Halton dominating and Connor Colby getting dominated. After an encouraging start, Colby is officially a problem. Seattle attacked him, and what’s particularly cool is that I was able to really track that effectively. Because I logged Byron Murphy II and Leonard Williams as elite players (same for Demarcus Lawrence in the run game), we were able to identify that Seattle got Colby isolated against one of that elite pairing consistently. And he consistently lost. It’s one of the cooler reflections of tape to data thus far this season…..Keion White was a menace, and Romello Height is very clearly starting to cook, club and all. Mykel Williams also had a basic bull rush pressure that became White’s sack. It’s worth noting that Williams exclusively played on the edge this week. That’s easing him back into it. I would be stunned if that doesn’t change as the season goes.”

title: Kyle Shanahan wants Raheem Morris with 49ers ‘for as long as I’m here’
summary: The San Francisco 49ers had a big coordinator change this offseason, as they dealt with the depature of Robert Saleh after just one season as the team’s defensive coordinator. The move was a big loss for the 49ers, but it allowed Kyle Shanahan to team up with Raheem Morris once again for the first time […]
full_text: (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers had a big coordinator change this offseason, as they dealt with the depature of Robert Saleh after just one season as the team’s defensive coordinator. The move was a big loss for the 49ers, but it allowed Kyle Shanahan to team up with Raheem Morris once again for the first time in a decade. In fact, Shanahan had thought about Morris as his defensive coordinator when initially hired by the 49ers in 2017, but the Atlanta Falcons wanted to keep him as their coordinator. So, the dream only finally came true this offseason following Morris’s departure from the Falcons, and it’s been a beaming success so far. Despite dealing with a ton of young talent and injured personnel, Morris has the 49ers as the NFL’s third-best defense in EPA allowed per play and points allowed per game. He’s been able to put his own sprinkles on the defense, while we’re seeing players out there with a ton of confidence, notably in the secondary. Morris’s background is different from his predecessors. Robert Saleh and DeMeco Ryans both had linebacker backgrounds, while Morris was a defensive back in college and has coached the position throughout his career. Has that difference shown up with the 49ers secondary so far? “Yeah, I think it definitely does,” Shanahan said of Morris’s background. “It also has to do with different schemes. When you play our true three-deep, four-under that we played for nine years with true zone drops instead of match drops and just our type of two shells and stuff, you get used to who’s supposed to stop plays. When you have zoning linebackers always underneath between the numbers and stuff, DBs don’t have to quite be as aggressive. “But, then when you blitz, they need to. I think just from a schematic standpoint and from the first day of OTAs, those guys aren’t counting on linebackers so they have to be more aggressive in coverage. When you do that throughout OTAs, throughout training camp, you just naturally get more aggressive and better at stuff. Then sometimes we do have our linebackers under it, but they’re not always counting on them. They might be there sometimes, they might not. Those guys are playing concepts and stuff to stop plays without any help and that’s been their edge. I think it’s made them better. It’s given them more confidence in practice and I think that’s what we’re all seeing in games.” That confidence has especially been seen in the 49ers’ cornerback room. Renardo Green has enjoyed a huge bounce-back year and just had two interceptions on Sunday against the Seattle Seahawks. Both Deommodore Lenoir and Upton Stout are playing at a good level. Malik Mustapha has bounced back after an up and down sophomore season. And even with Ji’Ayir Brown’s ups and downs, we’re seeing him make plays as well. That’s not all, though. The 49ers have found ways to get pressure, despite being down a large group of linemen. Linebackers Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw are playing at a high level. As a whole, the defense has really been clicking, and that’s even against teams like the Seahawks, Broncos, and the Los Angeles Rams. With how Morris has coached, there have already been the early questions of how long the 49ers can keep him. But, since he’s been a head coach twice in his career, there may be more of a pause for external teams to hire him. Kyle Shanahan doesn’t plan on moving on anytime soon. “I see Raheem here for as long as I’m here,” Shanahan added. “And if I wasn’t, I’m sure they wouldn’t be getting rid of him either. Raheem’s so good of a coach, you’ve always got to be nervous you’ll lose him as a head coach. But, if that doesn’t happen I don’t plan on him ever leaving. So, got to make sure that happens.”
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: 3 things to watch for in 49ers-Commanders: Keep Jayden Daniels in the pocket
summary: The San Francisco 49ers look to extend their five-game winning streak against the Washington Commanders on Monday Night Football at Levi’s Stadium. The Commanders limp into this game with an injury report longer than the 49ers’ somehow and following a tie with the New York football Giants. After a very physical and tense matchup with […]
full_text: (Photo by Greg Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers look to extend their five-game winning streak against the Washington Commanders on Monday Night Football at Levi’s Stadium. The Commanders limp into this game with an injury report longer than the 49ers’ somehow and following a tie with the New York football Giants. After a very physical and tense matchup with the defending Super Bowl champions, the extra day of rest is right on time for the 49ers. Seattle fell to the Broncos last night, so a win on Monday night will place an even tighter hold on the NFC West for San Francisco. There is no shortage of storylines heading into Monday. Brandon Aiyuk could have been at the top of them, but yeah, you know how that went. Adam Peters returns to Santa Clara, as does former first-round pick Javon Kinlaw, who has turned in a solid career as a professional. Here are three things to watch for on Monday night: The 49ers rushing attack vs. Washington’s run defense Among all the issues with the Commanders in 2026, the front seven isn’t among them. The overall defense for Washington has earned a zero in EPA, which means the defense isn’t a positive, but it isn’t a detriment. The scales tip based on the Commanders’ run defense, as the passing defense has been torched. Washington allows -0.07 EPA/rush, and the passing defense allows 0.05 EPA/pass. The interesting part is the game plan may be closer to the vest on Monday night given the injuries to the receiver position. Mike Evans missed Thursday’s practice with soreness in his Achilles. The 49ers may be inclined to run the football and try to hit that magic 30-carry number, but Washington is solid at defending the run. Will the 49ers throw it around the yard and test Fabian Moreau or Mike Sainristil? Amik Robertson has done a great job so far in 2026, but the secondary around him is very susceptible to the pass. Defending Jayden Daniels It doesn’t matter the season, defensive coordinator, or personnel; the 49ers have issues defending mobile quarterbacks. Daniels rushing ability kept Washington alive last Sunday against the Giants. Washington’s offense is never under center at 37.7%, which is the third-lowest total in the NFL. Out of shotgun is where the Commanders live at 53.9%. The 49ers will need to keep Daniels in the pocket and make him work from the pocket. Improvising outside of the pocket opens things up for Daniels to run and get the ball to players downfield if the coverage breaks down. Disciplined pass rush will be the key to containing Daniels. Washington’s left tackle issues The loss of Laremy Tunsil can’t be understated. Tunsil was a massive upgrade for Washington’s offensive line. His absence hasn’t been easy to deal with, as third-year tackle Brandon Coleman has stepped in for Tunsil and is responsible for 32.2% of Washington’s allowed pressures, the highest number in the NFL. This season, Coleman has allowed 18 pressures, 13 hurries, two QB hits, and three sacks on 203 pass-blocking snaps. Ouch. His latest performance against the Giants was his worst of the season, with two sacks, two hurries, and four pressures allowed on 39 pass-blocking snaps. Whoever is lined up against Coleman has to take advantage. The 49ers have a chance to continue the pass rush surge we saw on Sunday against Seattle. title: John Lynch says George Kittle asked him if the 49ers were trading for a pass rusher
summary: San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch was asked if trade talks around the league are increasing and whether there are more calls in a Friday morning interview on KNBR: “Just because the flow of the way the trade deadline is approaching, yes. That’s our job to do that. To talk with our counterparts around […]
full_text: Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch was asked if trade talks around the league are increasing and whether there are more calls in a Friday morning interview on KNBR : “Just because the flow of the way the trade deadline is approaching, yes. That’s our job to do that. To talk with our counterparts around the league. We receive calls. We make calls. Just to kind of see where the market is at. I think the answer to that is yes. We’re just doing our jobs.” When asked if Lynch could tell us if he was talking to the Los Angeles Chargers about Khalil Mack, he laughed and said: “No, I can’t tell you that. I had a lot of people ask me that yesterday. We seem to be connected to everyone. I don’t know where that comes from. I had a player ask me that yesterday. It’s usually [George] Kittle. He asks about everything, which I love.” Khalil Mack is an obvious trade candidate for the 49ers. Mack said himself that San Francisco was this close to acquiring him in a trade way back in 2018 before the Chicago Bears swooped in at the last minute. Mack wouldn’t cost two first-round picks this time around. Depending on the salary retention, he could cost as low as a conditional Day 3 pick. The Chargers have little reason to hold on to the 35-year-old pending free agent at 0-5. Mack’s $10 million signing bonus has already been paid, so the 49ers would owe a little more than $6 million in 2026 salary. If you’re the 49ers, why not go younger? Mack’s teammate, Tuli Tuipulotu, is in the final year of his rookie deal. He was a second-rounder from the 2023 NFL Draft. On 10 fewer pass-rush snaps, Tuipulotu has five more pressures and a pass-rush win rate that’s five percentage points higher. He also has seven more run stops and forced two fumbles. Tuipulotu is 266 pounds, so he has no trouble holding up against the run. If the 49ers are looking at one of the Chargers’ pass rushers, the lesser-known name might be the better option.
author: Kyle Posey

title: John Lynch shares why the 49ers hit on a ‘real high rate’ on their late-round picks
summary: San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch joined Chriss Simms on the Unbuttoned podcast to discuss injuries, late-game management, and changes in defensive back play. Lynch also spoke about how the 49ers’ draft strategy changed and why they needed to add length to the defensive line: I think first of all, nobody’s perfect in the draft. It’s […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Matt Kartozian-Imagn Images | Matt Kartozian-Imagn Images San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch joined Chriss Simms on the Unbuttoned podcast to discuss injuries, late-game management, and changes in defensive back play. Lynch also spoke about how the 49ers’ draft strategy changed and why they needed to add length to the defensive line: I think first of all, nobody’s perfect in the draft. It’s an inexact science. But you better have a good process. I think Kyle and I having been here for 10 years now, we’ve got a lot of continuity. So sometimes, the faces change — Raheem Morris in for Robert Saleh. But we have a really good knowledge of what we like in players. And then, typically, in our schemes, you know. Because we go to great lengths to define each and every position and the characteristics at that position. Now, I’ll tell you, it changed a little bit this year with Raheem. We were going to be doing more 5-down fronts. And there was probably more of an emphasis this year. You look at some of the guys like [Jaden] Dugger, the linebacker that we took. We knew we had a bunch of little Chihuahuas that would chase you and swarm you. We needed some length, you know, to play those fronts. And whether we had gone to more of the 5-down fronts or not, we needed some length in there. A guy like Gracen Halton, we just loved his style. He’s an attack-defensive lineman. We loved his film from Oklahoma. I really think why we hit on late-round picks exceptionally well is because we have great synergy with our coaching staff. Scouting, coaching. It’s still baffling knowing that Halton fell to Day 3 of the NFL Draft. He’s a hair under 6’3″ and sub-300 pounds. I get it. But he tested like a superb athlete in the areas that translate for defensive linemen: Lower-body explosiveness. He wasn’t an under-the-radar prospect, either. He started on arguably the best defense in the country. Then he went out and had a good Senior Bowl week. Not to mention, he’s only 22. Lynch talked about why the team hits on late-round picks: We talk about alignment all of the time. That’s where you use data. Our R&D, our research and development, when they’re in on a player, when scouting is in on a player, when coaching is in on a player, we hit at a real high rate. And a lot of those late round picks, when you have that alignment on a guy, you say, “Alright. We don’t think he’s going until here.” Now we’ve gotta be really skillful and use our experience as to when we do think we can get him. And then sometimes getting lucky, like with Brock Purdy. The follow-up questions to that would be why there isn’t the same synergy for early-round picks, which department has the lowest hit rate on Day 1 and Day 2. Why not implement more of whatever it is that allows you to find talents like Halton, Dugger, or Malik Mustapha earlier in the draft?

The rebuilding Titans are in full-blown evaluation mode. Continuing to evaluate the young talents on this roster has become the most important must-achieve in yet another wasted campaign. We’ve identified three young Titans who are most worth analyzing versus the Colts in Week 6. QB Cam Ward Titans QB Cam Ward was a mixed bag versus the Houston Texans. He received little support from his teammates, with the offensive line and skill players making constant mistakes, including a Tyjae Spears fumble and several dropped passes. WR Carnell Tate Rookie wide receiver Carnell Tate failed to build on his breakout performance. LB Anthony Hill Jr. Rookie linebacker Anthony Hill Jr. has arguably written the most positive story of this miserable 2026 Titans season. The former Texas Longhorns standout has posted a team-high 47 tackles. In fact, Hill ranks sixth in the entire NFL in tackles. title: Dan Quinn, hot seats & 18%: Commanders fan reaction to the Giants tie
summary: A child of the last millennium When I was a young kid — near the middle part of the 20th century — we didn’t have the Super Bowl. The NFL’s championship game wasn’t officially called the Super Bowl until January 1969, just months ahead of the first Apollo moon landing, and the name was retroactively […]
full_text: ASHBURN, VA - AUGUST 12: Head coach Dan Quinn of the Washington Commanders speaks with the media during a joint practice at BigBear.ai Performance Center on August 12, 2026 in Ashburn, Virginia. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images A child of the last millennium When I was a young kid — near the middle part of the 20th century — we didn’t have the Super Bowl. The NFL’s championship game wasn’t officially called the Super Bowl until January 1969, just months ahead of the first Apollo moon landing, and the name was retroactively given to the first two AFL-NFL championship games that had been played in calendar years 1967 and 1968. Back then, in my early childhood, before the Super Bowl era of the NFL had begun, the league’s origins didn’t really feel very far in the past — after all, the National Football League had been born at about the same time as my father! Even major league baseball wasn’t much older than my grandfather . Somehow, as a late-postwar ‘baby boom’ kid in the early 1960s, I still felt a connection to games and players of decades past that, today, are barely even considered relevant to the modern games and the digital age. But I was that nerdy kid who used to read books about the history of football and baseball with incredible voracity ( though not too nerdy; I also played all the sports I read so much about ). I knew all about Ty Cobb, Bronco Nagurski ( who could only be stopped ’with a shotgun as he’s leaving the dressing room’ ), Babe Ruth, Jim Thorpe, Red Grange, the Nippy Jones shoe-polish pitch that happened a scant 3 years before I was born, and the cry of “Say it ain’t so, Joe” from the 1919 World Series. Knowing all that about my childhood connection to the (then) not-so-distant early days of American professional sports, it’s probably not surprising that an apocryphal saying about baseball reverberates with me; here it is, paraphrased from an episode of The West Wing : “They say you’re guaranteed to win 54 games and guaranteed to lose 54 games, but it’s the 54 in the middle that decide the pennant. I just wish somebody would circle those games on the calendar so we’d know when to try.” Data, inertia, and the fluid-54 The humor in that wry statement about the baseball season is obvious, I hope, but there’s also a more universal truth in there as well; specifically, that there’s a certain amount of inertia in data samples, where the real action is in the fluid middle, not at the more static extremes. Let me try to explain what I mean. Reacts surveys Over the years that I’ve been responsible for authoring the Hogs Haven Reacts surveys and publishing their results, the weekly in-season confidence question has often made me think of this longstanding observation about wins, losses, and that fluid middle-54 in major league baseball. I guess what I mean is that — with respect to our Hogs Haven surveys — even when things are generally going well for the team, a certain percentage of fans will express a lack of confidence; by the same token, even when things are going poorly, a certain percentage of fans seem to remain optimistic in their outlook about the team. Most of the time, it seems to me, the story I end up writing is focused on the thoughts of survey respondents who comprise that fluid middle — the fans whose optimism or pessimism (in a given week) is driven largely by the team’s W-L record and recent on-field performance. It’s their constantly-changing mood that I typically find myself attempting to capture, understand, and explain from week to week. Captain Jack In some seasons, that middle group has been so large that it reminded me of the movie, Pirates of the Caribbean: At World’s End , where Jack Sparrow gets the entire crew to sprint back and forth across the deck in unison, rocking the Black Pearl until it completely flips over. Entrenched Pollyannas and Cassandras This season, the confidence (or lack of confidence) has been slightly more stable than that. On each end — the “Pollyannas” and the “Cassandras” — there has been a stable group comprising about 15% to 20% of survey respondents who’ve either maintained confidence despite problems (Pollyannas), or, alternately, have remained pessimistic even when good things have happened (Cassandras). That has left about 60% to 70% of survey respondents swinging back and forth in response to the latest news — an impressively large group, to be sure, but not enough to — metaphorically speaking — flip over the Black Pearl . There’s a surprising amount of ballast at each end of our survey. Surprisingly, not a total loss of faith Reading many of the headlines this week in the wake of the tied game vs the NY Giants, I had the feeling of a cataclysmic disaster taking place in Ashburn; a complete loss of faith based on the final 12 seconds of that overtime contest. These survey results don’t really reflect that, though. The 18% of survey respondents still professing to have confidence in the team’s direction isn’t significantly different than the result following the Week 2 loss to the Cowboys in Dallas. Honestly, I’d been expecting the survey results this week to show an absolute meltdown in confidence to near-0%. Instead, roughly 1 in 6 survey respondents continue to see a team headed in the right direction. Visit our partners at FanDuel Cassandra’s view We know which issues are of concern to the 82% who lack confidence. The Cassandras argue that Quinn has mismanaged critical game situations, failed to mentor or assist his rookie offensive coordinator (David Blough), and relies on high energy/passion over sound X’s and O’s. They (mostly) want Quinn fired immediately. Opinions on GM Adam Peters are more nuanced and divided, with many commenters urging patience, pointing out that he inherited a legacy of mediocrity and mismanagement, and feeling that AP deserves at least a couple more seasons to finish building the foundation, while critics argue the roster remains one of the lowest-rated in the league, pointing to poor pass-rush production, lack of player development, and questionable durability among free-agent additions. A number of critics have noted that other heavily injured teams (like the 49ers) have managed to stay competitive, leading some to question the team’s conditioning, depth, and overall roster quality. How about Pollyanna? But what things are on the minds of the Pollyannas that comprise 18% of this week’s survey respondents? For many, having a true dual-threat franchise quarterback is the primary reason to believe the team is heading in the right direction. Fans praise Jayden Daniels’ vision, recent enhanced willingness to protect himself from injury, and pure football speed as an elite foundation for the rest of the roster. Others advocate for patience with young offensive coordinator David Blough, arguing that detours and growing pains are an expected part of a long-term rebuild. A number of those who continue to express confidence in the direction of the team also seem more inclined to see a method to the manner in which Adam Peters is building the roster, along with improving roster-building skills from year to year for the 3rd-year GM. Differing perceptions of time and achievement When I try to analyze the dynamic at work in these survey results, I think an important factor that separates the Pollyannas and Cassandras is their relative perception of time — as in, how long it should take the leadership (owners, GM, coaches) to shed the dysfunction of the Snyder era, re-build the hollow roster left behind by Ron Rivera, and field a consistent playoff contender on the field. Those still seeing the team through burgundy-colored glasses seem to perceive a construction project underway that isn’t complete, but has that strong foundation mentioned above in Jayden Daniels. They tend to see 2025 as an outlier driven by some poor roster decisions that haven’t been repeated, and a plague of injuries that also adversely impacted the Commanders in Weeks…

title: We may never know full story of Commanders end-of-game events vs. Giants
summary: Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough was the latest in a line of players and coaches to talk about that Week 5 tie with the Giants where the clock was unfathomably allowed to run out before giving Drew Stevens a chance to convert a makable field-goal attempt.   Like head coach Dan Quinn and quarterback Jayden […]
full_text: Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough was the latest in a line of players and coaches to talk about that Week 5 tie with the Giants where the clock was unfathomably allowed to run out before giving Drew Stevens a chance to convert a makable field-goal attempt. Like head coach Dan Quinn and quarterback Jayden Daniels before him , he stood up and took responsibility for what went down. Blough said he thought extensively about the play and how he could’ve done better, emerging with resolve that the Commanders will do what’s required to fare better in the future. The messaging is sound. The shielding of others makes sense, though it’s clear many share blame in what happened against the Giants. The Commanders are ready to move on, as they should be with the unbeaten 49ers up next. The topic will continue to come up, especially when GM Adam Peters gives his weekly 106.7-FM radio appearance on Monday morning and against during the Monday Night Football broadcast. What we shouldn’t expect to hear, though, is anything new. There was some hope for more details on the communication breakdown or the order of operations that led to this mess. There was hope Blough might shed some light on key facets, but he didn’t offer much. The unified front was retained. If there are no Sunday morning show leaks, that’s another plus that Quinn is holding the Commanders together. But… Did the Commanders know they had zero timeouts, as guard Chris Paul and Sam Cosmi alluded to earlier? Blough didn’t say in an answer to Ben Standig’s question about it. It’s suspect, considering the lack of urgency getting back to the line of scrimmage, but we don’t know. Why substitute so late, with no timeouts and less that a minute left, going from 11 personnel to 13 personnel? “Whether it’s an advantageous look we saw earlier in the game,” Blough said, “or we’re trying to get to something helping the kick at the end…” What was the intent of the play, a shot down the field with Chig Okonkwo and Treylon Burks working deeper, or a chance to get a few extra yards with a pass to Ben Sinnott on the left sideline? “Every play has different intent, but, with the way the weather was shaping out and how the kicking game had been on both sides with the field conditions,” Blough said, “we really wanted to help out the kick. It wasn’t good enough for our unit, starting with me.” The Commanders can't get the play off in time and this game ends in a tie pic.twitter.com/WmPp6q5hU0 — NFL (@NFL) October 11, 2026 Not knowing everything is part of being an NFL football fan. Or even a football reporter. You can watch the tape and infer and listen to players and coaches, but we’re never going to fully get to the bottom of this case. The puzzle will always be missing a few pieces. That’s both aggravating and part of the deal. It makes sense for Blough to stay quiet on personnel groupings he thinks could work against a Giants team Washington will play in the future, or keeping the intent of a play quiet when they play New York a second time. While we want to know every little thing, competitive advantage between teams is a real thing, and Commanders opponents will scour every camp video and press conference looking for an edge. That’s a real fact. And, in the matter of Blough, while he was a key part of this whole thing, it shouldn’t alter Commanders fans’ impressions of him overall at this point. He’s a 31-year-old rookie play caller and creative mind still learning on the job. Could Quinn have added an older senior offensive assistant to help? Maybe. Maybe not. Week 5 proved a costly lesson, but the guy is smart and well-composed and sure seems to be pragmatic. There’s confidence he’ll learn and be better for this. “For me in particular, how do you handle that situation better then next time you’re in it?” Blough said. “It’s a scar that we all wear but we move forward. That’s all you can do.”

title: David Blough: It falls on me…I’m the leader of the unit
summary: The Washington Commanders are preparing for a Monday Night Football game against the San Francisco 49ers, but still getting asked about the finish to last week’s game against the Giants. This is the first time the media has had a chance to question Washington’s coordinators, but we’ve heard from Dan Quinn three times since the […]
full_text: The Washington Commanders are preparing for a Monday Night Football game against the San Francisco 49ers, but still getting asked about the finish to last week’s game against the Giants. This is the first time the media has had a chance to question Washington’s coordinators, but we’ve heard from Dan Quinn three times since the final play of overtime was bungled, resulting in a tie. There have been a lot of questions, assumptions, speculation, and third-hand reporting about what led to that breakdown in communication, and who gets the blame for the inexplicable outcome of a game Washington should have won. Offensive coordinator David Blough said he’s the last line of communication with the QB, and it falls on him. He was asked about switching personnel with time ticking away, and said they could have done some things differently in that situation. Everyone wants to know the intent of the last play, and if they were trying to score a touchdown. Blough didn’t want to disclose much, but said they were trying to help the kick due to the weather and kicking conditions on the day. Jayden Daniels came back from a two-week absence, and had a very good game. Blough said he looked spectacular at times, and he was happy with what he saw on the field. Daniels had his foot stepped on during the final play, and it wasn’t the first time this season. Chris Paul also stepped on his foot before he dislocated his elbow, and Blough said they are evaluating everything, but that’s definitely an area they’re looking to get cleaned up. Another area is pre-snap penalties that continue to get called against Washington. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 16 October 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Commanders links Definition of dual-threat pic.twitter.com/1g3R4iKvV3 — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) October 16, 2026 Articles The Athletic (paywall) Jayden Daniels takes blame for Commanders’ botched final play: ‘Ultimately, it’s on me’ “Ultimately, it’s on me at the end of the day,” Daniels said Thursday. “I know DQ (coach Dan Quinn) is getting a lot of flak for it and whatever. But regardless of what happens, I’m the person on the field who is supposed to calm everything, control everything, and I failed to (meet) the standard I hold myself to and the standard of the organization.” Daniels said he addressed his teammates and made it clear to them that “it’ll never happen again.” The baffling sequence made the Commanders the biggest talking point in the NFL, with former players (and one current player) as well as ex-coaches and team executives weighing in on social media and elsewhere. “I can’t say (the criticism is) not warranted because of what happened,” he said. “… Marcus kind of told me — I’m not gonna say I’m one of the greats, but he told me every great one has been through adversity in their career. And you gotta deal with it. You gotta learn from it and move forward and not dwell on it and let it affect you. Obviously, as a competitor, as a person, you feel like you let everybody around you down. But I have a great team and people in the locker room who have my back and uplift me in those moments. And ultimately, I’m the one that has to take ownership of it and move forward from it.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated The Commanders need to (immediately) solve what ailed them against the blitz last Sunday Daniels was still sacked four times against the blitz, and there were plays when the protection could have been better. It just means blaming those sacks entirely on the players up front would ignore what Daniels and Quinn both said Thursday. There are two ways to look at how Washington handled the pressure against New York. Daniels completed more than 60% of his passes against the blitz and made the Giants pay with his legs, but New York also had enough late success to keep bringing it throughout the fourth quarter and overtime. The Giants found something that worked when they needed it most. San Francisco will see the same film, and the 49ers won’t have to blitz on nearly three-quarters of Washington’s late-game dropbacks to find out if the Commanders fixed anything. A few pressure looks in the right situations should be enough to test Daniels’ checks and whether the rest of the offense is on the same page. Considering how the Giants ended Sunday’s game, Washington should expect that test to come. Follow the action and share every cheer, question and instant reaction with fellow fans on the SB Nation app. Chat live during every game Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly move between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Sports Illustrated ‘It Is F—ing Chaos’: How NFL Teams Prepare for Clock-Management Situations Albert Breer surveys current and former head coaches about voices in their headset and what it’s really like when the clock is ticking After Rachaad White ran off right guard to bleed the clock, Daniels let it run down from 51 seconds to 12, snapping the ball with three seconds left on the play clock. He then ran into the line, hit the deck with eight seconds to go and laid there for three more. You know the rest . “No doubt, Dan Quinn went over that,” another head coach in the league said this week. “That is 100% the quarterback’s fault. But the head coach, that’s what we get paid for.” Of course, Quinn was never going to say that about Daniels. Nor should he. He is indeed paid to fall on such swords. And the reality is, for all the work that these guys do … stuff happens. [T]he question arises of how many voices should be in the head coach’s ear on Sundays. Most coaches say it should only be one or two. Two head coaches I spoke with had an analytics director and an offensive assistant as the two on the headset when it comes to game management. Another has his game-management coordinator alone. O’Brien, at BC, has former Browns head coach Rob Chudzinski and offensive analyst Andrew Breiner as his guys. And the headset to the quarterback cuts off at 15 seconds. How the 25 seconds before that are used is, of course, vital. And sometimes, like in a two-minute situation, they actually have less than that to relay the call to the players. “You want to have a lot of clarity, for sure,” said one head coach. “There’s no doubt. And that’s where it’s just like, you got to stay calm in those situations. Like, We practice it. We’ve been here. We good? Yeah, we’re good .” Unfortunately, as more people have gotten involved, with the rise in analytics across the NFL, the more potential there is for a crash out—when folks hired for expertise in these areas and coaches alike are trying to be heard at the most critical time. “Yeah, it’s chaos,” said another head coach, about such situations that aren’t routine, but can arise. “The coordinator’s gotta have discipline. I mean, it is f—ing chaos. It’s like, Everyone, shut the f— up .“ [He] then added that the one thing that shouldn’t have ever changed, as the access to data around game management has, is that access to the head coach on the topic should be very limited—“It’s one voice that’s the person you’ve been communicating with all week that you need to communicate with.” So, then, who’d be to blame in the Washington situation? “I don’t know if we’ll ever know,” the coach answered. “You can, as a head coach, say all the right things. But at the end of the day, if he doesn’t do it, you can’t out him.” What you can do, of course, is review what went wrong, something the Commanders did this week, as they cleared the wreckage of the end of the Giants game. One thing that was clear: It didn’t happen for a lack of trying. The same way a Sirianni decision Sunday , on a kickoff, failed despite the Eagles’ coach being maniacal on situational ball—according to those who’ve been around him— Quinn’s team faltered in the big moment hours later, despite having an entire camp built on handling these in-game situations. So much so, in fact, that over the course of camp, Quinn had the play clock for the aforementioned 11-on-11 work start at 38 seconds, rather than the normal 40, to speed up his players a bit, so they’d be more comfortable in the chaos of a game. Daniels is smart. He didn’t forget the lessons learned. The work was done. Sometimes, stuff happens. But the Commanders desperately need him to bring some stability to their cornerback room. title: Stats and Snaps – NFL Week 5: Giants @ Commanders
summary: I count myself among the more optimistic Washington Football fans since Josh Harris took over ownership from the Shrek villain. Nevertheless, last Sunday’s failure to beat the Giants strained my ability to keep a positive outlook, even more than the previous week’s loss to the Colts. The reason for that was the team’s sheer determination […]
full_text: I count myself among the more optimistic Washington Football fans since Josh Harris took over ownership from the Shrek villain. Nevertheless, last Sunday’s failure to beat the Giants strained my ability to keep a positive outlook, even more than the previous week’s loss to the Colts. The reason for that was the team’s sheer determination to avoid winning, despite multiple advantages working in their favor and opportunities left on the field. The failure of clock management in the final series of the game has been discussed at length, so there is no need to re-litigate that here. However, even prior to the Commanders possessing the ball on the Giants’ 24 yd line, with 12 sec remaining in overtime, the franchise was working hard to find ways to deny itself the victory. In the two games prior to Sunday’s embarrassing 27-27 overtime tie with the Giants, the Commanders’ run blocking collapsed, leaving them unable to establish a running game with lead back Bill Croskey-Merritt. Against the Giants, the run blocking was much improved – not just due to the return of Sam Cosmi to the line-up, but across the board. In the first half, Bill rushed for 51 yds and a TD, averaging 7.3 Y/A. For some reason, the Commanders turned away from the run in the second half and overtime, giving Bill just 4 touches in 3 quarters of football, and none in overtime – even as he increased his average 7.8 Y/A in the second half. The mid-game adjustments on defense mirrored those on offense. Warren Sharp of Sharp Analytics has pointed out how the Commanders switched coverage from a scheme which was working in the first half, and allowed Jameis Winston to lead a comeback: you can talk about the late game botch, but Dan Quinn screwed up the game for the Commanders well before that first half, Quinn went 22% man coverage & 50% 2-high (#5 highest) held Jameis Winston 4.5 YPA, 44% comp & -0.58 EPA/att it worked but in the second half, despite… pic.twitter.com/vTLi6aSRPh — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) October 13, 2026 For what seems like an eternity, Washington fans have been wishing for a coaching staff with the ability to make adjustments when game plans aren’t working. Against the Giants, they inexplicably adjusted game plans which were working, with predictable results. It was the type of effort which gets coaches fired. The tie gave the Commanders sole possession of last place in the division, with a 1-3-1 record. Head coach Dan Quinn is running out of opportunities to turn the season around. Hopefully, he and his coaching staff have learned the lessons which can be drawn from the disappointing tie, which should have been a win. Despite the result, there were some flashes of promise which the team might be able to build on against the 49ers, including standout performances by Jayden Daniels (up to the last play), Bill Croskey-Merritt, Sam Cosmi, K’Lavon Chaisson, Daron Payne, Sonny Styles and Amik Robertson and great plays from many of their teammates. With key players like Nick Cross and Trey Amos potentially returning from injury, the heat under Quinn’s seat might provide the motivation he needs to lift his game and take the fight to the heavily favored 49ers. But before we get ahead of ourselves, let’s take a final look at who played where, who stood out, and who showed areas for improvement in the Commanders’ tie with the New York Giants. Stats & Snaps Going on Hiatus: The Stats and Snaps will be taking a two week holiday, and will return after the Eagles game on November 1. In its place, I will be doing a 1/3 season stats roundup of the Commanders’ players during the week before the Eagles game. BIGGEST PLAYS OF THE GAME These plays had the largest impact on teams’ scoring potential within a drive, as judged by Expected Points Added (EPA). Threshhold: EPA = +/- 2.25 Biggest Plays for Commanders Q3, 7:56, 2 nd and 6 at NYG 38: Jayden Daniels scrambles up the middle for 38 yards, touchdown. EPA 4.22 Q4, 11:13, 3 rd and 2 at NYG 26: Jayden Daniels scrambles left tackle for 26 yards, touchdown. EPA 3.86 Q1, 13:07, 1 st and 10 at NYG 33: Jacory Croskey-Merritt up the middle for 33 yards, touchdown. EPA 3.62 Q2, 0:07, 4 th and 10 at WAS 39: Dominic Zvada 57 yard field goal no good. EPA -2.72 Q1, 7:15, 4 th and 12 at WAS 32: Dominic Zvada 50 yard field goal no good. EPA -2.84 OT, 8:01, 4 th and 8 at WAS 28: Dominic Zvada 46 yard field goal no good. EPA -2.92 OT, 2:00, 1 st and 10 at WAS 24: Cam Skattebo up the middle for no gain. Cam Skattebo fumbles, recovered by Shy Tuttle at WAS-24 (tackle by Sonny Styles). EPA -4.45 Q2, 2:09, 2 nd and 8 at NYG 47: Jameis Winston sacked by K’Lavon Chaisson for 8 yards. Jameis Winston fumbles (forced by K’Lavon Chaisson), recovered by Tim Settle at NYG-28 and returned for 1 yard. EPA -5.43 Biggest Plays for Giants Q4, 7:24, 4 th and 8 at WAS 17: Jameis Winston pass complete short middle to Isaiah Likely for 17 yards, touchdown. EPA 4.69 Q3, 5:35, 4 th and 4 at WAS 43: Jameis Winston pass complete short right to Tyrone Tracy for 21 yards. EPA 3.71 Q3, 1:47, 3 rd and 9 at WAS 10: Jameis Winston pass short middle is intercepted by Amik Robertson at WAS-1 and returned for no gain. Penalty on Amik Robertson: Defensive Pass Interference, 9 yards. EPA 3.67 Q4, 1:48, 1 st and 10 at WAS 17: Jameis Winston pass complete deep middle to Malik Nabers for 17 yards, touchdown. EPA 2.56 Q1, 10:23, 3 rd and 13 at NYG 40: Jameis Winston pass complete short left to Isaiah Likely for 15 yards. EPA 2:42 Q3, 0:47, 3 rd and 3 at WAS 3: Jameis Winston pass complete short right to Isaiah Likely for 3 yards, touchdown. EPA 2.28 OT, 0:15, 2 nd and 8 at NYG 24: Jayden Daniels sacked by Tremaine Edmunds for no gain. EPA -3.57 OFFENSE A big question on Jayden Daniels ’ return from injury was whether he would be able to run with a brace on his left arm. The Commanders’ star QB answered that one by leading the team in rushing, with an impressive 103 yds, 2 TDs and 4 first downs in 9 attempts (11.4 Y/A; 55.6% success rate). His rushing total was the 7 th highest in Week 5 at any position, and he was one of three players with over 100 rushing yds and 2 rushing TDs. JD5 was also effective in the air, completing 17/25 attempts (68%, ADOT 8.2 yds) for 199 yds, 0 INT and 0 TD (40% success rate). He was sacked 5 times for 23 yds and faced 15 total pressures (40.5% of dropbacks), per PFF, but did a good job of protecting the ball and avoiding turnovers. His mental lapse on the last play of overtime did negate an opportunity to go for a game winning field goal. But that is not recorded on the stat sheet. Daniels was also penalized 5 yards for delay of game in overtime. Aside from those mistakes, Daniels had an excellent game. His 80.9 total QBR ranked 5 th best among starting QBs in Week 5. Advanced rushing stats (YBC, broken tackles) were sourced from PFR Jacory Croskey-Merritt was curiously second in playing time, despite being by far the most effective running back in the game. Bill bounced back from a string of unimpressive performances to post his best game of the season, toting the rock 11 times for 82 yds (7.45 Y/A), 1 TD and 4 first downs, with 1 broken tackle. His 63.6% rushing success rate was the 5 th highest among NFL players in Week 5 (min 10 attempts). Bill got most of his action in the first half (7 att, 51 yds, 1 TD), got light duty in the second half (4 att, 31 yds), and did not get a touch in overtime. Bill’s rebound most likely had a lot to do with a big improvement in run blocking, as measured by PFF grades (see OL, below). Consistent with that take, he averaged a whopping 5.3 yards before contact/attempt this week, up from 0.4 YBC/att against the Colts and 1.0 YBC/att against the Seahawks. Rachaad White had 9 carries for 18 yds and no first downs (2.57 Y/A, 42.9% success rate), while averaging just 1 YBC/att. He caught his lone target as a receiver for 2 yds. White was penalized 5 yds for a false start in the 2 nd quarter. It was just the second penalty of his…

title: Washington Commanders vs. Niners on MNF Week 6: Inside the Matchup
summary: Back in June and early July, HH veteran writer Bill-in-Bangkok, offered a week-by-week preview via the 5 O’Clock Club of the Washington Commanders regular season schedule for 2026. As we roll into the actual games during the regular season, Hogs Haven will revisit each of these previews with John Portis adding additional thoughts and updates […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MD - DECEMBER 31: Terry McLaurin #17 of the Washington Commanders runs with the ball against the San Francisco 49ers during the first half of the game at FedExField on December 31, 2023 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images Back in June and early July, HH veteran writer Bill-in-Bangkok, offered a week-by-week preview via the 5 O’Clock Club of the Washington Commanders regular season schedule for 2026. As we roll into the actual games during the regular season, Hogs Haven will revisit each of these previews with John Portis adding additional thoughts and updates as we go inside the matchup to get you ready for every opponent the Commanders face in 2026. From John Portis: The Washington Commanders enter Week 6 coming off one of the worst clock management gaffes in team history. After tying the Giants this past Sunday, the 1-3-1 Commanders will be looking to get their second win of the season as the team takes on the San Francisco 49ers on Monday Night Football. Back in July , Bill-in-Bangkok predicted a hot start to the season for the Niners but seems to have underestimated their win total, as San Francisco narrowly defeated the Seattle Seahawks 32-29 last week to remain undefeated. 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan was expected to have one of the best offenses in football, but key injuries to several players, including wide receivers Rickey Pearsall, Demarcus Robinson, Christian Kirk and rookie De’Zhaun Stribling, have limited the team’s potential. News got worse for the Niners last week, as Deebo Samuel was ruled out with a hamstring injury and is expected to miss an extended period of time. Free-agent addition Mike Evans, who is fighting through a rib injury and now Achilles soreness, is playing at a high level and leads the team with 24 receptions for 326 receiving yards and three touchdowns. Quarterback Brock Purdy has made up the difference for the depleted wide receiver corps by playing at an MVP level, and his 85.5 QBR through the first five weeks leads the league. While Christian McCaffrey and George Kittle are starting to slow down, they are still very talented, and the Niners rank 3rd in team offense . Shanahan’s offense was always expected to be good, but San Francisco’s defense has been the real surprise of the 2026 season. After losing Robert Saleh to the Titans, the 49ers turned to Raheem Morris to coordinate their defense. So far, Morris looks to be an upgrade for them and has improved the team’s performance in multiple defensive categories. The 49ers offense was expected to be one of the best in the NFL. But through 5 games the defense ranks 3rd in EPA per play; 4th in scoring; 5th in yards allowed per play; 6th in net yards per pass attempt; 7th in rushing yards allowed per play; and 8th in opponent passer rating. — Matt Maiocco (@MaioccoNBCS) October 13, 2026 The improvement is even more impressive given the team has been without edge rusher Nick Bosa, a player Shanahan indicated has a chance to return this week , although Dre Greenlaw’s suspension was upheld and the linebacker will miss Monday night’s game. San Francisco has made explosive plays on offense while limiting them on defense, and the 49ers are playing well on both sides of the ball, which is why the team remains undefeated headed into Week 6. Explosive Play Rates through Week 5 BUF’s offense and SF’s defense in a league of their own. pic.twitter.com/320dhHAQSU — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) October 13, 2026 The challenge may seem insurmountable for Washington, but one of the positives from last week is that Jayden Daniels appears to have no limitations following his second left-elbow dislocation. The Commanders’ franchise quarterback was spectacular last Sunday and recorded 199 passing yards with a 68% completion rate, along with 103 rushing yards and 2 TDs on 8 rushes. Running back Bill Croskey-Merritt also demonstrated his explosive potential behind an improved offensive line with a 33-yard touchdown run and another 22-yard rush to set up one of Jayden Daniels’ touchdowns. Bill is dealing with a groin injury but could still sit up Monday night. Week 5 Explosive Plays Shows how many runs of 10+ yards and passes of 20+ yards each offense produced. Buffalo leads the league with 13 this week. pic.twitter.com/vhuLfjEJ3o — Gridiron Stats and Info (@GridironInfo_) October 13, 2026 Washington’s run defense continues to be ranked in the top 10 , and the possible return of Trey Amos and Nick Cross could bolster a secondary that has struggled this season . Both players practiced in full yesterday. Washington’s front seven will need to do a better job of generating pressure against an offensive line that allowed zero sacks through the first four weeks of the season, although Seattle’s defense was able to get home last Sunday, generating 3 sacks and 3 turnovers while limiting the 49ers offense to 269 yards, 14 first downs, and an average of 4.8 yards per play. The most important component for head coach Dan Quinn and his players will be the belief they can win in Santa Clara on Monday night. Amik Robertson’s early response this week would indicate that they have the needed belief. Chin up.. Chest Out. New Week, New Opportunity. — Amik Robertson (@_YoungTruth7) October 13, 2026 B etting Lines Oddsmakers have established the home team as the solid favorite for this matchup. Point Spread : 49ers -7.5 Game Total (Over/Under) : 50.5 points Bill-in-Bangkok’s original preview published July 5th: Date: October 19, 2026, 8:15 p.m. ET (Monday Night Football) Location: Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, California The 49ers are off to Australia to open their season by playing Thursday Night Football in Victoria at the historic Melbourne Cricket Ground, where I once watched Day 5 of a test match between South Africa and the Aussies (which Australia won handily). San Fran then plays 3 home games in a row (presumably as payback for the Australia travel) before a short road trip to Seattle. They return to Levi’s Stadium for the MNF game against Washington — their 4th home game in 5 weeks! The Niners should have at least a couple of wins on the board as they play the Cardinals and Dolphins in two of those home games (who were ranked 29th & 32nd, respectively, in ESPN’s latest Football Power Index ). They may not be above .500, however, since their 3 other games are NFC & AFC West contests against the Rams, Seahawks and Broncos. We know that Kyle Shanahan always feels a little extra motivation against Washington, where he felt he and his dad got the metaphorical bum’s rush out the door at the end of the 2013 season, the senior Shanahan’s final NFL coaching job after a probable Hall of Fame NFL coaching career. Kyle Shanahan and John Lynch are two of the most petty individuals in the NFL. Washington gave San Fran the best LT and a future HOFer for a hot pocket and an extra large dill pickle because that’s where HE wanted to be traded to. Kyle still being petty after all these years… — Mark Tyler (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) June 25, 2026 The All-Time Series Numbers Dating back to 1952, San Francisco and Washington have played each other 36 times, including 4 playoff games. The Niners have had the best of both regular season and postseason, winning 3 of the 4 playoff games, and holding onto a commanding 23-12-1 lead overall. Washington’s sole playoff win over the 49ers came in the NFC Championship game after the 1983 season. Things have been a little less one-sided since 2017, with Washington winning 2 out of 5 regular season games. You may remember the not-so-classic mud bowl played in Landover during monsoon rain in 2019 when the 49ers won 9-0. The last time Washington beat the 49ers, they were branded as the “Football Team” in the 2020 COVID-affected season. This will be the first meeting between the two teams in the AP/DQ/JD5 era (though not the first of the Josh Harris ownership), so Dan Quinn will be looking to get off on the right foot against his former…

title: NFL Week 6 predictions: Upsets, fantasy sleepers, stat lines, TD scorers, more
summary: First touchdown of 2026 for Drake London? Aaron Rodgers climbing the NFL record books? The Texans pulling an upset? Let's predict 15 things for Week 6.
full_text:
Week 6 of the  2026 NFL season is underway after the Broncos beat the Seahawks in overtime Thursday night . But what will happen in the remaining 13 games? We have 15 predictions from our NFL experts.

 First, betting analyst Pamela Maldonado picks three underdogs who could win outright. Then, analytics writer Seth Walder projects stat lines for three players. Fantasy football writer Eric Moody suggests three sleepers, and analyst Matt Bowen predicts three players who will find the end zone. Finally, analyst Ben Solak lays out three wild-card predictions.

 Could the Texans pull off an upset in London? How many sacks will Chiefs defensive tackle Chris Jones have against the Chargers? Could Rams tight end Tyler Higbee be a sneaky play in fantasy? Will Falcons wide receiver Drake London find the end zone for the first time this season? And will Aaron Rodgers move up in the NFL record books against the Bucs? Let's make 15 big predictions for the Sunday and Monday action.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Upset picks | Projected stat lines 
 Fantasy sleepers, surprises 
 TD scorers | Other predictions 

 
 

 Maldonado predicts three upsets 
 

 Dallas Cowboys +1.5 (+102 moneyline) at Green Bay Packers 

 The Packers have allowed the eighth-fewest passing yards per attempt this season, but this matchup presents a much tougher test than the backup quarterbacks they've faced in the past two weeks. The Cowboys convert nearly half their third downs and lead the league in the percentage of possessions producing points. Green Bay can hit big plays, but the Cowboys have enough on offense with Dak Prescott , CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens to answer.

 
 

 

 New York Giants +1.5 (+108 moneyline) vs.  New Orleans Saints 

 The Giants have a way to make this Sunday easier for quarterback Jameis Winston . They can run against a struggling Saints defense, then move tight end Isaiah Likely out wide for easy throws over smaller defenders.

 On the other side, Saints QB Tyler Shough has struggled even when he has time to throw. So New York doesn't need to constantly pressure him to get stops. That gives the Giants enough to keep this close and win at home.

 
 

 Houston Texans +3 (+120 moneyline) vs. Jacksonville Jaguars 

 Jacksonville's defense is allowing just 14 points per game, but opponents are still finding room to throw. The Jaguars allow 7.7 yards per attempt and 93.2 yards per game to No. 1 receivers, giving QB C.J. Stroud and WR Nico Collins a matchup to attack in London on Sunday .

 Houston can also pressure  Trevor Lawrence  without blitzing or disguising its coverage, making it harder for the quarterback to read the defense. That gives the Texans a way to get stops while leaving more players in coverage.

 

 

 Walder predicts three stat lines 
 

 Sauce Gardner , CB, Indianapolis Colts : 28 coverage snaps, 3 targets, 0 receptions allowed 

 Gardner has had a rough season, allowing 1.3 yards per coverage snap and 10.3 EPA when targeted. But I think most of that has been due to on-ball results, rather than Gardner putting himself in poor position throughout the route.

 Gardner has allowed a plus-19% completion percentage over expected, while spending 24% of the time in tight coverage (fourth most among outside CBs with at least 100 coverage snaps). And my own player tracking analysis indicates Gardner has been in good position before the ball is thrown. All of this is to say that his start to the season might be a blip, and a game against the Titans is just what he needs to turn the results around.

 
 

 Chris Jones , DT, Kansas City Chiefs : 1.5 sacks, 5 pressures, 26% pass rush win rate 

 Jones has the privilege of facing Chargers right guard Cole Strange in Week 6 , which ought to present more than enough opportunities for Jones to get at QB Justin Herbert . Strange has just a fourth percentile pass block win rate this season; Herbert is taking sacks at a massive 9.7% clip.

 Jones' season is off to a quiet start with zero sacks and a 59th percentile pass rush win rate at defensive tackle. He can kickstart his year against Strange -- and have an even bigger day if right tackle Joe Alt ( neck ) is out again.

 

 
 

 Michael Wilson , WR, Arizona Cardinals : 34 routes, 6 targets, 2 receptions, 12 receiving yards 

 Marvin Harrison Jr . was traded  to the Texans, so Wilson is in for a production explosion, right? That might happen ... but only after this week against the Rams .

 Wilson could see a healthy dosage of  Trent McDuffie  -- if the Rams' top cornerback plays (he is questionable with a groin injury). McDuffie is allowing 0.4 yards per coverage snap in 2026 -- well below the 1.1 average for an outside cornerback, per NFL Next Gen Stats. Plus, he has spent 28% of his time in tight coverage, which puts him third in that stat -- one spot above the aforementioned Gardner.

 Wilson has a 93 catch score in ESPN's receiver scores , which means he's good in contested catch situations. But he is struggling to get separation from defenders (47 open score). It is likely going to be a tough afternoon for him.

 

 

 Moody predicts three fantasy sleepers 
 

 Kirk Cousins , QB, Las Vegas Raiders (41.8% rostered in ESPN leagues) 

 Cousins disappointed with just 13.7 fantasy points against the Patriots last week , but he has averaged 18.5 fantasy points per game this season. He has a favorable matchup against a Bills defense that has allowed the fourth-most fantasy points per game to quarterbacks and the most to wide receivers.

 
 

 Kendre Miller , RB, New Orleans Saints (21.9%) 

 Miller is on the flex radar against the Giants after leading the Saints' backfield with 10 carries for 9.0 fantasy points last week. Alvin Kamara was dealing with a back injury in that game (and Travis Etienne Jr . has been on IR for the past two weeks), so Miller could see more touches if Kamara remains limited. The Giants' defense has allowed the ninth-most rushing yards per game this season.

 
 

 Tyler Higbee , TE, Los Angeles Rams (11.2%) 

 Higbee has seen at least six targets and scored 11 or more fantasy points in each of the past three games, including a 20.2-point performance in Week 3 . The Rams lead the league with 43.8 pass attempts per game, and this week's matchup against the Cardinals has one of the highest projected point totals on the slate (51.5 on DraftKings). Arizona has also allowed the fifth-most fantasy points per game to tight ends this season.

 

 

 

 Bowen predicts three touchdown scorers 
 

 Drake London , WR, Atlanta Falcons 

 London has yet to find the end zone this season, but he's averaging seven catches and 136 receiving yards over the past three games. He will see plenty of man coverage from the Bears secondary Sunday (55.3% of coverage snaps), and he will have clear advantages on the perimeter.

 
 

 Cam Skattebo , RB, New York Giants 

 Skattebo hasn't scored a touchdown since Week 1 , but he has the volume and matchup to change that against the Saints . Skattebo has 18 or more carries in three games, with at least 15 touches in all five. New Orleans has given up a league-worst 10 rushing scores this season. I think Skattebo gets in on a goal-line carry here.

 
 

 Javonte Williams , RB, Dallas Cowboys 

 Williams has rushed for at least one touchdown in four games this season, and his 11 carries inside the 5-yard line are tied for the most in the league with Jahmyr Gibbs and Derrick Henry . I expect Williams to see scoring opportunities versus a Green Bay defense that has allowed eight rushing touchdowns this season, the second most in the league.

 

 

 Solak makes three more predictions 
 

 Browns WR Denzel Boston will have his first 100-yard game 

 The Browns rookie reminds me a lot of the Falcons' Drake London, who just put up 118 yards on the Ravens' secondary across seven catches. Boston has the blend of size, hand strength and technique that allows him to win in the layers between defensive zones, where the Ravens have really…
